questions.simple: Imagine a jar of marbles bought at different prices. When you add marbles, the average price per marble changes. When you give some away, the average stays the same, there are just fewer marbles. The query walks through trades one by one, carrying the jar's count and average forward.
questions.remember: Recursive WITH = carry yesterday's answer into today's row.
questions.why: A weighted average cost depends on the previous row's computed values, which a plain window SUM cannot express once sells are mixed in. Recursive WITH seeds the first trade and joins each new trade on rn = previous rn + 1, carrying hold_qty and avg_cost forward. Oracle requires the column alias list on a recursive subquery factoring clause.
questions.tip: When each row needs the previous row's computed result, not just its raw value, I use recursive WITH or MODEL instead of LAG.

steps.say: Step one. Number the trades in time order.
steps.find: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY trade_time) AS rn

steps.say: Step two. The anchor: the first trade sets the holding and the average price.
steps.find: SELECT rn, trade_no, side, qty, price FROM t WHERE rn = 1

steps.say: Step three. Each next trade joins to the previous result. Buys add quantity, sells take it away.
steps.find: CASE t.side WHEN 'B' THEN r.hold_qty + t.qty
steps.to: FROM r JOIN t ON t.rn = r.rn + 1

steps.say: Finally, for a buy, the new average mixes old and new cost. For a sell, the average stays.

questions.title: Customers holding a gold loan
questions.scenario: Sunita Rao, gold loan desk head at a Pune branch, wants to call every customer who has a gold loan. Some customers have more than one gold loan.
questions.schema:
CUSTOMER(cust_id VARCHAR2(5), cust_name VARCHAR2(30), city VARCHAR2(20))
LOAN(loan_id VARCHAR2(5), cust_id VARCHAR2(5), loan_type VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(12,2))
-- loan_type: GOLD, HOME, PERSONAL; amount in INR
questions.output_note: Chetan has two gold loans but appears once, because IN only checks membership.
questions.task: List cust_id and cust_name of customers who have at least one GOLD loan, each customer once, ordered by cust_id.
questions.hint: Put the gold-loan customer ids in a subquery and filter with IN.
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id, cust_name
FROM customer
WHERE cust_id IN (SELECT cust_id
                  FROM loan
                  WHERE loan_type = 'GOLD')
ORDER BY cust_id;
questions.simple: Think of a teacher with a list of children who brought a lunch box. She reads the class register and ticks a name if it is on that list. Even if a child brought two lunch boxes, the name is ticked once. The subquery makes the list, and IN checks each customer against it.
questions.remember: IN = "is this name on the list?"
questions.why: The subquery returns the set of cust_id values with a GOLD loan, and IN keeps each CUSTOMER row whose cust_id is in that set. Because the filter is on the outer table, duplicates in LOAN do not multiply rows, unlike an INNER JOIN. Oracle typically turns this into a semi-join.
questions.tip: When I only need to check existence in another table, I use IN or EXISTS instead of a join, so I never get duplicate rows.

steps.say: Step one. The inner query lists every customer id that has a gold loan.
Step two. The outer query keeps a customer only if their id is on that list. Chetan shows once, not twice.
Finally, sort the result by customer id.

questions.title: UPI count by app and status
questions.scenario: Rahul Iyer from the UPI operations team wants a quick daily summary. For each UPI app, how many payments succeeded or failed, and for how much.
questions.schema:
UPI_TXN(txn_id VARCHAR2(5), app_name VARCHAR2(15), status VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(12,2))
-- status: SUCCESS or FAILED; amount in INR
questions.task: Show app_name, status, the number of payments (txn_count) and their total amount (total_amt) for every app and status pair, ordered by app_name then status.
questions.hint: List both columns in GROUP BY, so each app-and-status pair becomes one group.
questions.solution:
SELECT app_name, status,
       COUNT(*)    AS txn_count,
       SUM(amount) AS total_amt
FROM upi_txn
GROUP BY app_name, status
ORDER BY app_name, status;
questions.simple: Imagine sorting coins into boxes, one box for each colour and size together, like 'big gold' and 'small gold'. Then you count the coins in each box and add up their value. GROUP BY with two columns makes one box for every app and status pair, then COUNT and SUM work inside each box.
questions.remember: Two columns in GROUP BY = one row per pair.
questions.why: GROUP BY app_name, status forms one group per distinct combination of the two columns. COUNT(*) and SUM(amount) are then computed separately inside each group. Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list must appear in the GROUP BY, or Oracle raises ORA-00979.
questions.tip: Every column I select that is not inside an aggregate must also be in GROUP BY.

steps.say: Step one. Group the payments by app and status together, so each pair becomes one box.
Step two. Inside each box, count the payments and add up the amounts.
Finally, sort by app name and then status.

questions.concept: Latest row per key with tie-break
questions.title: Current status of each motor policy
questions.scenario: Meera Pillai in motor insurance servicing needs today's status of each policy. A policy can get two status changes on the same day, so the date alone cannot decide.
questions.schema:
POLICY_STATUS(policy_no VARCHAR2(5), status VARCHAR2(12), status_date DATE, seq_no NUMBER(6))
-- one row per status change; seq_no always increases, so a higher seq_no is the later change
questions.output_note: MP1 lapsed and was revived on the same day; seq_no 3 breaks the tie, so REVIVED wins.
questions.task: Show policy_no, status and status_date of the latest status per policy. Latest means the highest status_date; on the same date, the highest seq_no. Order by policy_no.
questions.hint: Use ROW_NUMBER with PARTITION BY policy_no and ORDER BY status_date DESC, seq_no DESC, then keep row 1.
questions.solution:
SELECT policy_no, status, status_date
FROM (
  SELECT ps.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY policy_no
                            ORDER BY status_date DESC, seq_no DESC) AS rn
  FROM policy_status ps
)
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY policy_no;
questions.simple: Think of a diary where you write what happened each day, and some days have two entries. To know the latest news, you open the last page and read the bottom entry. ROW_NUMBER numbers each policy's entries from newest to oldest, using the entry number to break same-day ties, and we keep entry number 1.
questions.remember: Latest per group = ROW_NUMBER, newest first, keep 1.
questions.why: ROW_NUMBER restarts at 1 for each policy_no and orders rows by status_date DESC, then seq_no DESC, so the tie on 10-09-2026 is resolved deterministically. Filtering rn = 1 must happen in an outer query because window functions cannot appear in WHERE. Without the seq_no tie-breaker, Oracle could return LAPSED or REVIVED for MP1 on different runs.
questions.tip: I always add a unique tie-breaker column to ROW_NUMBER's ORDER BY, otherwise "latest" is not deterministic.

steps.say: Step one. For each policy, number the status rows from newest to oldest.
steps.to: ORDER BY status_date DESC, seq_no DESC) AS rn

steps.say: Step two. On the same date, the higher sequence number counts as later. That makes revived beat lapsed.
steps.find: ORDER BY status_date DESC, seq_no DESC) AS rn

steps.say: Finally, keep only row number one, the current status of each policy.

questions.title: Average CIBIL score by branch
questions.scenario: Credit manager Arjun Bhatia compares applicant quality across branches. New-to-credit applicants have no CIBIL score, stored as NULL, and must not drag the average down.
questions.schema:
BUREAU_SCORE(app_id VARCHAR2(5), branch VARCHAR2(15), cibil_score NUMBER(3))
-- cibil_score is NULL for new-to-credit (NTC) applicants
questions.output_note: Indore averages (760 + 700) / 2 = 730, not 1460 / 3. Nashik has only NULL scores, so its average is NULL.
questions.task: Per branch, show applicants (all rows), avg_score (average of scores rounded to a whole number, ignoring NTC) and ntc_count (applicants with no score). Order by branch.
questions.hint: AVG already skips NULLs; NTC count is COUNT(*) minus COUNT(cibil_score).
questions.solution:
SELECT branch,
       COUNT(*)                       AS applicants,
       ROUND(AVG(cibil_score))        AS avg_score,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(cibil_score)  AS ntc_count
FROM bureau_score
GROUP BY branch
ORDER BY branch;
questions.simple: Imagine three friends in a race, but one did not run. To find the average time, you only add the two who ran and divide by two. AVG does the same: blank scores are left out completely. If nobody in a branch has a score, the average is blank too.
questions.remember: AVG skips NULLs: they are not zero.
questions.why: Aggregate functions except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs, so AVG(cibil_score) divides by COUNT(cibil_score), not COUNT(*). A group with only NULLs returns NULL from AVG, as Nashik shows. Using AVG(NVL(cibil_score, 0)) would wrongly count NTC applicants as score 0.
questions.tip: I check whether a NULL should mean "unknown" or "zero" before averaging; AVG treats it as unknown and skips it.

steps.say: Step one. Count every applicant in the branch, with or without a score.
Step two. Average the scores. Blank scores are skipped, so Indore is seven sixty plus seven hundred, divided by two.
Finally, all rows minus scored rows gives the new-to-credit count.

questions.title: Reject RTGS requests below minimum
questions.scenario: Payments lead Kavita Menon loads RTGS requests in a batch. RTGS needs at least INR 2 lakh, enforced by a CHECK constraint. Bad rows must be logged, not stop the batch.
questions.schema:
RTGS_REQUEST(req_id VARCHAR2(4), acct_no VARCHAR2(8), amount NUMBER(14,2))
RTGS_OUT(req_id VARCHAR2(4), acct_no VARCHAR2(8), amount NUMBER(14,2) CHECK (amount >= 200000))
RTGS_REJECT(req_id VARCHAR2(4), reason VARCHAR2(30))
-- a CHECK violation raises ORA-02290

questions.hint: First SUM per variant and month, then ROW_NUMBER by issue_month and keep row 1.

  FROM card_issue
  GROUP BY card_variant, issue_month
), r AS (

)

FROM r
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY issued DESC;
questions.simple: Think of a new shop that opens branches in two towns in the same month. To know how good the opening month was, you add both towns' sales for that first month only. The query first adds up regions for each month, then picks each card's very first month, then sorts the best start on top.

questions.why: Picking the first row before aggregating would return only one region (700 or 500) for RUPAY_PLAT, so the CTE m sums across regions per variant and month first. ROW_NUMBER over issue_month ascending marks the launch month per variant, and rn = 1 keeps it. MIN(issue_month) with a join back is an alternative, but the window approach scans once.
questions.tip: In "first period" questions, I aggregate to the right grain before ranking, otherwise I rank partial rows.

questions.title: Net settlement between bank pairs
questions.scenario: Treasury analyst Vikram Shetty settles interbank payments once a day. Instead of paying both ways, each pair of banks should settle one net amount, and pairs that cancel out need no payment.
questions.schema:
INTERBANK_PAY(pay_id VARCHAR2(4), from_bank VARCHAR2(4), to_bank VARCHAR2(4), amount NUMBER(15,2))
-- from_bank owes to_bank the amount (INR); bank codes like SBIN, HDFC, ICIC
questions.output_note: SBIN owes HDFC 5000000 + 700000 and is owed 3200000, so it pays 2500000 net. ICIC and SBIN cancel to 0 and are dropped.
questions.task: For each pair of banks, compute the net amount owed. Show payer, payee and net_amount for pairs with a non-zero net, largest first.
questions.hint: Use LEAST and GREATEST to make one key per pair, sign the amount by direction, then SUM.
questions.solution:
WITH p AS (
  SELECT LEAST(from_bank, to_bank)    AS bank_a,
         GREATEST(from_bank, to_bank) AS bank_b,
         CASE WHEN from_bank < to_bank
              THEN amount ELSE -amount END AS signed_amt
  FROM interbank_pay
), n AS (
  SELECT bank_a, bank_b, SUM(signed_amt) AS net
  FROM p
  GROUP BY bank_a, bank_b
)
SELECT CASE WHEN net > 0 THEN bank_a ELSE bank_b END AS payer,
       CASE WHEN net > 0 THEN bank_b ELSE bank_a END AS payee,
       ABS(net) AS net_amount
FROM n
WHERE net <> 0
ORDER BY net_amount DESC;
questions.simple: Imagine you owe your friend 50 rupees and your friend owes you 32. Instead of swapping money twice, you just give 18. The query puts each pair of banks in alphabetical order so 'A to B' and 'B to A' land in the same box. Money one way is plus, the other way is minus, and the total tells who pays whom.
questions.remember: LEAST and GREATEST = one key for both directions.
questions.why: LEAST and GREATEST normalise (SBIN, HDFC) and (HDFC, SBIN) into the same ordered key, so both directions group together. The CASE gives a positive sign when bank_a pays bank_b and negative otherwise, so SUM is the net exposure of bank_a to bank_b. The final CASE uses the sign to choose payer and payee, ABS makes the amount positive, and net <> 0 removes pairs that fully offset.
questions.tip: For A-to-B versus B-to-A problems, I build an unordered pair key with LEAST/GREATEST and a signed amount.

steps.say: Step one. Put each bank pair in alphabetical order, so both directions share one key.
Step two. Money from the first bank to the second is plus. The other way is minus.
steps.to: THEN amount ELSE -amount END AS signed_amt

steps.say: Step three. Add up the signed amounts for each pair to get the net.
steps.find: SELECT bank_a, bank_b, SUM(signed_amt) AS net

steps.say: Finally, the sign decides who pays. Pairs that cancel to zero are dropped.

questions.title: When did Ramayana cross 500 crore?
questions.scenario: Neha works in analytics at a bank that processes a cinema chain's ticket payments. Her manager wants the day the film's India collection crossed 500 crore rupees, to plan a 500 crore club cashback offer. The numbers below are sample data.
questions.schema:
BOX_OFFICE(show_date DATE, collection_cr NUMBER(8,2))
-- one row per day, India collection in crore rupees (sample data)
questions.output_note: On 10 Nov the total went from 465 to 525, so only that day is marked. 11 Nov is above 500 too, but the day before was already above 500.
questions.task: Show each day's collection with a running total, and mark the first day the running total reached 500 crore as 'CROSSED 500'.
questions.hint: SUM() OVER (ORDER BY show_date) keeps adding day by day; running total minus today's value is yesterday's total.
questions.solution:
SELECT show_date, collection_cr,
       SUM(collection_cr) OVER (ORDER BY show_date) AS running_total_cr,
       CASE WHEN SUM(collection_cr) OVER (ORDER BY show_date) >= 500
             AND SUM(collection_cr) OVER (ORDER BY show_date) - collection_cr < 500
            THEN 'CROSSED 500' END AS milestone
FROM   box_office
ORDER  BY show_date;
questions.simple: It is like filling a piggy bank every day. Each day you add that day's money and check the total. On 10 November the total jumped from 465 to 525, so that is the day it crossed 500. The CASE checks two things: today's total is 500 or more, and yesterday's total was below 500.
questions.remember: Running total = SUM with OVER ORDER BY.
questions.why: SUM(collection_cr) OVER (ORDER BY show_date) uses the default frame RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, giving a cumulative sum. Subtracting the current row's value gives the previous running total, so the crossing day is where the previous total is below 500 and the current one is at least 500. No self-join or subquery is needed.
questions.tip: Running total minus today's value gives yesterday's total, so I can find the exact crossing day without a self-join.

trend.hook: Ramayana is ruling the box office, so let's find the day it crossed 500 crore!

steps.say: Step one. SUM with OVER, ORDER BY show date, adds each day's collection to the total so far.
steps.find: SUM(collection_cr) OVER (ORDER BY show_date) AS running_total_cr

steps.say: Step two. CASE checks that today's running total is five hundred or more.
And that yesterday's total, which is the running total minus today, was still below five hundred.
Only that one day gets the label CROSSED 500.
Finally, ORDER BY show date lists the days in order.

questions.title: GTA 6 pre-orders: which cities make 80%?
questions.scenario: Arjun runs card-offers at a bank whose cards were used for GTA 6 pre-orders. He wants the smallest set of cities that together bring 80 percent of pre-order revenue, to target a cashback campaign there. The numbers are sample data.
questions.schema:
GTA6_PREORDERS(order_id VARCHAR2(5), city VARCHAR2(30), platform VARCHAR2(10), amount_inr NUMBER(8))
-- one row per pre-order paid with the bank's cards (sample data)
questions.output_note: Delhi is included because the total was still below 80 percent before it (63.3). Bengaluru and Delhi tie on revenue, so city name breaks the tie.
questions.task: Show the cities, biggest revenue first, that together make up 80 percent of pre-order revenue, including the city that crosses 80 percent, with the cumulative percentage.
questions.hint: Group by city first, then a running SUM over revenue descending; keep cities whose running total before them was below 80 percent.
questions.solution:
SELECT city, revenue,
       ROUND(100 * running / total, 1) AS cum_pct
FROM (
  SELECT city, SUM(amount_inr) AS revenue,
         SUM(SUM(amount_inr)) OVER (ORDER BY SUM(amount_inr) DESC, city
                                    ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running,
         SUM(SUM(amount_inr)) OVER () AS total
  FROM gta6_preorders
  GROUP BY city
)
WHERE running - revenue < 0.8 * total
ORDER BY revenue DESC, city;
questions.simple: Line up the cities from richest to poorest, like children lining up by height. Walk down the line adding up their money. Keep going until you have 80 percent of all the money, and include the city that takes you past 80. Everyone after that is left out.
questions.remember: Pareto = running SUM sorted big to small.
questions.why: The inner query groups to city revenue, and SUM(SUM(amount_inr)) OVER (...) runs a window over the grouped rows. ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING plus city in ORDER BY makes tied cities add one at a time; the default RANGE frame would add tied rows together. running - revenue is the total before the current city, so the filter keeps the crossing city too.
questions.tip: I always add ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to running totals, because the default RANGE frame lumps tied values together.

trend.hook: GTA 6 is finally out, so let's see which cities spent the most on pre-orders!

steps.say: Step one. Inside, GROUP BY city adds up each city's pre-order revenue.
A window SUM over revenue, biggest first, gives the running total. ROWS makes tied cities count one at a time.
An empty OVER gives the grand total of all cities.
Step two. Keep a city if the total before it was still below eighty percent.
Finally, running divided by total gives the cumulative percentage.

questions.concept: Peak hour per group with RANK
questions.title: Avengers: Doomsday peak booking hour per city
questions.scenario: Priya in the bank's payments team watches card traffic when Avengers: Doomsday advance booking opened. She needs the busiest hour in each city, to plan server capacity for the next big release. The numbers are sample data.
questions.schema:
AD_BOOKINGS(booking_id VARCHAR2(5), city VARCHAR2(30), booked_at DATE, seats NUMBER(3))
-- one row per advance booking paid by card (sample data)
questions.output_note: Chennai has a tie (5 seats at 10 and at 11), so RANK keeps both hours.
questions.task: For each city, show the hour (HH24) with the most seats booked and the seats in that hour. If two hours tie, show both.
questions.hint: Group by city and hour, then RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY SUM(seats) DESC) and keep rank 1.
questions.solution:
SELECT city, booking_hour, seats
FROM (
  SELECT city,
         TO_CHAR(booked_at, 'HH24') AS booking_hour,
         SUM(seats) AS seats,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city
                      ORDER BY SUM(seats) DESC) AS rnk
  FROM ad_bookings
  GROUP BY city, TO_CHAR(booked_at, 'HH24')
)
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY city, booking_hour;
questions.simple: Think of a sports day where each school gets its own race. We count the seats booked in every hour, then hold a separate race inside each city. The hour with the most seats wins in that city. If two hours finish together, both get the gold medal, which is what RANK does.
questions.remember: Best per group = RANK OVER PARTITION BY, keep 1.
questions.why: GROUP BY city and TO_CHAR(booked_at, 'HH24') gives seats per city-hour. RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY SUM(seats) DESC) restarts numbering in each city and gives tied hours the same rank, so rnk = 1 returns all top hours. ROW_NUMBER would silently drop one of the tied hours.
questions.tip: I pick RANK over ROW_NUMBER when ties must all be shown, and say so in the interview.

trend.hook: Avengers: Doomsday bookings are open, so let's find the busiest booking hour!

steps.say: Step one. Inside, group by city and booking hour, and add up the seats.
RANK with PARTITION BY city starts a new race in every city, most seats first.
steps.to: ORDER BY SUM(seats) DESC) AS rnk

steps.say: The GROUP BY must use the same hour expression.
Step two. Keep only rank one. Tied hours both have rank one, so both stay.
Finally, sort by city and hour.

questions.title: Gold is falling: find the biggest daily drop
questions.scenario: Gold prices have been sliding, and Ravi in the bank's gold-loan team must recheck loan-to-value limits. He wants each day's change in the 24-carat rate and the day with the biggest fall. The prices below are sample data, not real rates.
questions.schema:
GOLD_RATES(rate_date DATE, price_10g NUMBER(8))
-- 24-carat rate in rupees per 10 grams, one row per day (sample data)
questions.output_note: The first day has no previous day, so its change is NULL. The biggest fall is the most negative change: minus 2900 on 18 November.
questions.task: For each day show the price, the change in rupees and in percent from the previous day, and mark the day with the biggest fall as 'BIGGEST FALL'.
questions.hint: LAG(price_10g) OVER (ORDER BY rate_date) gives yesterday's price; MIN(change) OVER () finds the biggest fall.
questions.solution:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT rate_date, price_10g,
         price_10g - LAG(price_10g) OVER (ORDER BY rate_date) AS change_rs,
         LAG(price_10g) OVER (ORDER BY rate_date) AS prev_price
  FROM   gold_rates
)
SELECT rate_date, price_10g, change_rs,
       ROUND(100 * change_rs / prev_price, 2) AS change_pct,
       CASE WHEN change_rs = MIN(change_rs) OVER () THEN 'BIGGEST FALL' END AS flag
FROM   d
ORDER  BY rate_date;
questions.simple: Imagine writing the gold price in a diary every evening. Each day you look back one line to yesterday's price and write down how much it went up or down. LAG is that look back. Then you scan the whole diary for the biggest drop and put a star next to it.
questions.remember: LAG = yesterday's value in today's row.
questions.why: LAG(price_10g) OVER (ORDER BY rate_date) returns the previous row's price, NULL for the first row. The CTE computes the change once so the outer query can reuse it. MIN(change_rs) OVER () with an empty window scans all rows, so the row equal to it is the biggest fall; the NULL first row is ignored by MIN.
questions.tip: I compute LAG once in a CTE and reuse it, instead of repeating the window expression three times.

trend.hook: Gold prices have been falling sharply, so let's find the biggest one-day drop!

steps.say: Step one. In the C.T.E., LAG fetches yesterday's price for every row.
steps.find: LAG(price_10g) OVER (ORDER BY rate_date) AS prev_price

steps.say: Today's price minus yesterday's gives the change in rupees.
Step two. Change divided by yesterday's price, times a hundred, gives the percentage.
MIN over an empty window finds the most negative change, and that row gets the BIGGEST FALL label.
Finally, sort by date.

questions.title: Customers with a loan or a card
questions.scenario: Pooja in the cross-sell team wants one clean list of customers who hold a loan, a credit card, or both. Some customers appear in both lists, and she must not call them twice.
questions.schema:
LOAN_CUSTOMERS(cust_id NUMBER, cust_name VARCHAR2(30))  -- customers with an active loan
CARD_CUSTOMERS(cust_id NUMBER, cust_name VARCHAR2(30))  -- customers with a credit card
questions.output_note: Bilal and Divya are in both tables but appear only once, because UNION removes duplicate rows.
questions.task: List every customer who has a loan or a card, each customer only once, sorted by cust_id.
questions.hint: UNION combines two queries and removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them.
questions.solution:
SELECT cust_id, cust_name FROM loan_customers
UNION
SELECT cust_id, cust_name FROM card_customers
ORDER BY cust_id;
questions.simple: Imagine two class lists: the football team and the music club. Some kids are in both. If you want one list for a party invite, you write each name only once. UNION joins the two lists and crosses out the repeated names.
questions.remember: UNION = merge lists, drop repeats. UNION ALL = keep repeats.
questions.why: UNION applies a DISTINCT over the combined result, so identical rows from both branches appear once; this needs a sort or hash step. UNION ALL skips that step and is cheaper when duplicates are impossible or wanted. ORDER BY is written once, at the very end, and applies to the whole combined result.
questions.tip: I use UNION ALL by default and switch to UNION only when duplicates must really be removed, because the de-duplication costs extra work.

steps.say: Step one. Take every customer from the loan table.
Step two. UNION adds the card customers and removes anyone already listed.
Finally, one ORDER BY at the end sorts the whole combined list.

questions.title: Godzilla ticket sales by city
questions.scenario: Godzilla Minus Zero is roaring in cinemas, and Nikhil in the bank's cards team is tracking ticket payments made with its cards and UPI. He wants each city's total, highest first. All numbers are sample data.
questions.schema:
TICKET_BOOKINGS(booking_id NUMBER, city VARCHAR2(20), pay_mode VARCHAR2(10), amount NUMBER(8))
-- one row per paid movie booking, amount in rupees (sample data)
questions.output_note: Chennai has the single biggest booking, but Mumbai wins on total because it has three bookings.
questions.task: Show each city's number of bookings and total amount, with the highest total first.
questions.hint: GROUP BY city, then ORDER BY the SUM, using DESC for highest first.
questions.solution:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS bookings, SUM(amount) AS total_rs
FROM   ticket_bookings
GROUP  BY city
ORDER  BY total_rs DESC;
questions.simple: Think of three piggy banks, one for each city. Every ticket payment drops coins into its city's piggy bank. GROUP BY fills the piggy banks, SUM counts the money in each, and ORDER BY lines them up from fullest to emptiest.
questions.remember: GROUP BY makes the buckets; ORDER BY ranks them.
questions.why: GROUP BY city collapses the rows into one row per city, and SUM and COUNT are computed per group. ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so it can use the column alias total_rs. DESC sorts the largest total first; the default is ascending.
questions.tip: ORDER BY is evaluated last, so it is the one clause where I can use a SELECT alias like total_rs.

trend.hook: Godzilla Minus Zero is smashing the box office, so which city spent the most on tickets?

steps.say: Step one. GROUP BY city puts every booking into its city's bucket.
Step two. COUNT gives the bookings and SUM adds up the rupees in each bucket.
steps.find: SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS bookings, SUM(amount) AS total_rs

steps.say: Finally, ORDER BY the total, descending, puts the biggest city on top.

questions.title: Weekly NEFT totals, Monday to Sunday
questions.scenario: Farhan prepares a weekly NEFT volume report for operations. Weeks must run Monday to Sunday, and a Sunday payment must count in the week that started the Monday before.
questions.schema:
NEFT_TXNS(txn_id NUMBER, txn_date DATE, amount NUMBER(12))
-- outward NEFT payments, amount in rupees
questions.output_note: 22-11-2026 is a Sunday, so it belongs to the week starting Monday 16-11-2026.
questions.task: Show the Monday each week starts on, the number of payments and the total amount per week, oldest week first.
questions.hint: TRUNC(txn_date, 'IW') returns the Monday of the ISO week, whatever the session's NLS settings.
questions.solution:
SELECT TRUNC(txn_date, 'IW') AS week_start,
       COUNT(*)    AS txns,
       SUM(amount) AS total_rs
FROM   neft_txns
GROUP  BY TRUNC(txn_date, 'IW')
ORDER  BY week_start;
questions.simple: Think of a school timetable where every week starts on Monday. Whatever day a payment happens, you slide it back to that week's Monday and put it in that week's box. TRUNC with 'IW' does the sliding back, and GROUP BY fills the boxes.
questions.remember: TRUNC(date,'IW') = slide back to Monday.
questions.why: TRUNC(date, 'IW') truncates to the first day of the ISO week, which is always Monday. TRUNC(date, 'D') or 'DAY' depends on NLS_TERRITORY, so in the US setting a Sunday would start a new week. The GROUP BY must repeat the same expression, because the alias is not allowed there.
questions.tip: For weekly reports I use TRUNC with 'IW', because 'D' changes with the session's territory setting and can silently move Sundays.

steps.say: Step one. TRUNC with I W slides each date back to its Monday.
Step two. Group by that same Monday, so each week becomes one row.
Count and sum the payments in each week.
Finally, sort by the week start date.

questions.title: Higher of two bureau scores
questions.scenario: Leena's underwriting rule says: use the higher of the two credit bureau scores. But some applicants have only one score, and her first query gave them no score at all.
questions.schema:
BUREAU_SCORES(app_id VARCHAR2(5), cibil_score NUMBER(3), experian_score NUMBER(3))
-- NULL = score not received from that bureau
questions.output_note: GREATEST returns NULL if any argument is NULL, so A2 and A3 lose their score in the naive column. A4 has no score at all and correctly stays NULL.
questions.task: Show the plain GREATEST result as naive, and a correct best_score that uses the higher score, or the only score if one is missing.
questions.hint: Wrap GREATEST in COALESCE and fall back to each score.
questions.solution:
SELECT app_id,
       GREATEST(cibil_score, experian_score) AS naive,
       COALESCE(GREATEST(cibil_score, experian_score),
                cibil_score, experian_score) AS best_score
FROM   bureau_scores
ORDER  BY app_id;
questions.simple: Imagine two teachers each give you a mark, and you keep the higher one. If one teacher was absent, a fussy robot says 'I can't compare, so no mark!' COALESCE fixes that: if the robot gives up, just take whichever mark you do have.
questions.remember: GREATEST sees one NULL, returns NULL. COALESCE rescues it.
questions.why: In Oracle, GREATEST and LEAST return NULL as soon as any argument is NULL. COALESCE returns its first non-NULL argument, so when GREATEST fails it falls back to cibil_score, then experian_score. Using NVL(score, 0) instead would turn a missing pair into 0, which is a wrong, very low score.
questions.tip: I never default a missing credit score to zero with NVL; COALESCE around GREATEST keeps a truly missing score as NULL.

steps.say: Step one. Plain GREATEST works only when both scores are present.
Step two. COALESCE takes GREATEST's answer if it is not NULL.
Otherwise it falls back to whichever single score exists.
Finally, sort by application id.

questions.title: Fix swapped statement lines
questions.scenario: A migration bug swapped statement lines in pairs: line 1 with 2, line 3 with 4, and so on. Sunil must show the corrected order. If the last line has no partner, it stays where it is.
questions.schema:
STATEMENT_LINES(line_id NUMBER, narration VARCHAR2(40))
-- line_id is 1, 2, 3 ... with no gaps
questions.output_note: Line 5 is odd and is the last line, so it has no partner and keeps id 5.
questions.task: Return each narration with its corrected line id: odd ids move up by one, even ids move down by one, except a last odd line, which stays. Sort by corrected id.
questions.hint: MOD(line_id, 2) tells odd from even; compare with MAX(line_id) for the last line.
questions.solution:
SELECT CASE
         WHEN MOD(line_id, 2) = 1
              AND line_id = (SELECT MAX(line_id) FROM statement_lines) THEN line_id
         WHEN MOD(line_id, 2) = 1 THEN line_id + 1
         ELSE line_id - 1
       END AS corrected_id,
       narration
FROM   statement_lines
ORDER  BY corrected_id;
questions.simple: Imagine kids standing in a line, but every pair swapped places by mistake. Kid 1 should be kid 2, and kid 2 should be kid 1. So odd numbers step forward one, even numbers step back one. If the last kid has no partner, he just stays put.
questions.remember: Odd goes up one, even goes down one, lonely last stays.
questions.why: MOD(line_id, 2) = 1 identifies odd ids, which become id + 1, and even ids become id - 1. The scalar subquery MAX(line_id) catches an odd last row, which would otherwise point to an id that does not exist. This relies on ids being gapless; with gaps you would first renumber with ROW_NUMBER.
questions.tip: Before using id arithmetic I state the assumption that ids are gapless, and otherwise renumber with ROW_NUMBER first.

steps.say: Step one. An odd line that is also the last line has no partner, so it keeps its id.
steps.to: AND line_id = (SELECT MAX(line_id) FROM statement_lines) THEN line_id

steps.say: Step two. Every other odd line moves up by one.
Even lines move down by one.
Finally, sort by the corrected id to see the right order.

questions.concept: Compound return with EXP SUM LN
questions.title: Sensex rally: compound treasury returns
questions.scenario: The Sensex has been rallying, and Kiran on the treasury desk tracks the bank's ₹5 crore index-fund holding. He needs the compounded return to date, not a simple sum of daily percentages. Returns below are sample data, not real market figures.
questions.schema:
INDEX_RETURNS(trade_date DATE, ret_pct NUMBER(5,2))
-- daily return of the index holding in percent (sample data)
questions.output_note: Simply adding the daily returns gives 3.6 percent, but compounding gives 3.64 percent, because each day's gain builds on the previous days' gains.
questions.task: For each day show the daily return, the compounded return to date in percent (2 decimals), and the value of a ₹50,000,000 starting holding (rounded to the rupee).
questions.hint: SQL has no running PRODUCT, but EXP(SUM(LN(x))) multiplies the values.
questions.solution:
SELECT trade_date, ret_pct,
       ROUND(100 * (EXP(SUM(LN(1 + ret_pct / 100))
                    OVER (ORDER BY trade_date)) - 1), 2) AS cum_ret_pct,
       ROUND(50000000 * EXP(SUM(LN(1 + ret_pct / 100))
                    OVER (ORDER BY trade_date))) AS value_rs
FROM   index_returns
ORDER  BY trade_date;
questions.simple: Imagine a plant that grows a little each day, and each day's growth is a percentage of its new size, not its old size. So you can't just add the percentages; you have to multiply. SQL can add but can't multiply down a column, so we use a math trick: logs turn multiplying into adding, and EXP turns it back.
questions.remember: Running product = EXP of running SUM of LN.
questions.why: Compounded growth is the product of (1 + r) factors, and Oracle has no PRODUCT aggregate. Since LN(a*b) = LN(a) + LN(b), a running SUM of LN(1 + r/100) followed by EXP gives the running product. LN fails for factors of zero or below, so this works for returns above minus 100 percent only.
questions.tip: For compounding I use EXP(SUM(LN(1+r))) as a window, and I mention it breaks for a factor of zero or less.

trend.hook: The Sensex is rallying hard, so let's compound a treasury desk's daily returns in SQL!

steps.say: Step one. Turn each daily percent into a growth factor, like one point zero one two, and take its log.
Step two. A running SUM of logs, ordered by date, adds up all days so far.
EXP turns the summed logs back into the multiplied factor, so minus one, times a hundred, is the compounded return.
Finally, the same factor times five crore gives the holding's value each day.

questions.title: Which standing instructions missed?
questions.scenario: Rekha runs the monthly ₹2,500 standing-instruction debit with FORALL. One account id in the batch was closed and deleted, and the UPDATE silently matched nothing. She must log every id that updated zero rows.
questions.schema:
SI_ACCOUNTS(acct_id NUMBER, balance NUMBER(12))  -- accounts with a standing instruction
SI_LOG(acct_id NUMBER, msg VARCHAR2(40))  -- exceptions log, empty before the run
questions.output_note: SI_LOG after the run. In SI_ACCOUNTS, 501, 502 and 503 drop by 2500 to 17500, 5500 and 12500; 504 was not in the batch and stays 3000.
questions.task: Write a block that debits 2500 from accounts 501, 502, 599 and 503 with one FORALL, then logs 'ACCOUNT NOT FOUND' for every id whose UPDATE touched zero rows.
questions.hint: SQL%BULK_ROWCOUNT(i) holds the rows affected by the i-th FORALL execution; read it before running any other SQL.
questions.simple: Imagine a teacher hands out stickers to a list of kids all at once. Afterwards she checks a little tally card: how many stickers went to each name? One name got zero, because that kid has left the school. SQL%BULK_ROWCOUNT is that tally card, one count per name.
questions.remember: BULK_ROWCOUNT(i) = rows changed by the i-th FORALL run.
questions.why: FORALL sends all four UPDATEs in one context switch, and SQL%ROWCOUNT only gives the overall total of 3. SQL%BULK_ROWCOUNT(i) gives the count for each element, so element 3 (id 599) shows 0. The missing ids are collected first, because any new SQL statement, like an INSERT inside the loop, would overwrite the SQL% cursor attributes.
questions.tip: After FORALL I read SQL%BULK_ROWCOUNT into a collection first, because the next DML statement resets the implicit cursor attributes.

steps.say: Step one. One FORALL sends all four debits to the database in a single trip.
Step two. SQL percent BULK ROWCOUNT of i tells how many rows each debit touched.
Ids that touched zero rows are saved in a collection, before any other SQL runs.
Finally, a second FORALL writes the missing ids to the log, and we commit.

questions.concept: INSTEAD OF trigger on join view
questions.title: Update nominees through a view
questions.scenario: The policy servicing screen updates POLICY_NOMINEE_V, an outer-join view of policies and nominees. Anand needs updates to change an existing nominee, or add one when the policy has none yet.
questions.schema:
POLICIES(policy_no VARCHAR2(8), holder VARCHAR2(30))
NOMINEES(policy_no VARCHAR2(8), nominee_name VARCHAR2(30), relation VARCHAR2(10))
-- view: SELECT p.policy_no, p.holder, n.nominee_name, n.relation
--       FROM policies p LEFT JOIN nominees n ON n.policy_no = p.policy_no
questions.output_note: NOMINEES after both updates. LP1002's nominee was changed (MERGE matched); LP1003 had no nominee row, so the trigger inserted one.
questions.task: Write an INSTEAD OF UPDATE trigger on POLICY_NOMINEE_V that updates the nominee if one exists or inserts it otherwise, then run the two updates shown.
questions.hint: Inside the trigger, MERGE into NOMINEES using :NEW.policy_no from dual.
questions.solution:
CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER trg_policy_nominee_v
INSTEAD OF UPDATE ON policy_nominee_v
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  MERGE INTO nominees n
  USING (SELECT :NEW.policy_no AS policy_no FROM dual) s
  ON (n.policy_no = s.policy_no)
  WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET n.nominee_name = :NEW.nominee_name,
               n.relation     = :NEW.relation
  WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT (policy_no, nominee_name, relation)
    VALUES (:NEW.policy_no, :NEW.nominee_name, :NEW.relation);
END;
/

UPDATE policy_nominee_v SET nominee_name = 'Anil Menon', relation = 'BROTHER'
WHERE  policy_no = 'LP1002';
UPDATE policy_nominee_v SET nominee_name = 'Meera Iyer', relation = 'SPOUSE'
WHERE  policy_no = 'LP1003';
COMMIT;
questions.simple: Think of a school notice board that shows each student with their guardian's name. You can't write on the notice board itself; it's just a display. So a helper stands in front of it: when you ask to change a name, the helper goes to the real register and fixes it, or adds a new line if there was none. The INSTEAD OF trigger is that helper.
questions.remember: INSTEAD OF trigger = do the real work behind a view.
questions.why: An outer-join view is not reliably updatable, and a row with NULL nominee columns has no NOMINEES row to update at all. An INSTEAD OF trigger, which is always row-level, replaces the DML on the view with your own code. MERGE on :NEW.policy_no updates an existing nominee or inserts a new one, so both cases work through one UPDATE statement.
questions.tip: When an application must write through a complex view, I give it an INSTEAD OF trigger rather than changing the application to hit base tables.

steps.say: Step one. The trigger fires instead of the update on the view, once for each row.
Step two. MERGE looks for a nominee row with the same policy number.
If one exists, it is updated with the new name and relation.
If not, a new nominee row is inserted.
Finally, the screen just updates the view, and the trigger handles both policies.

questions.title: Top three FDs, ties included
questions.scenario: Priya, a branch manager, is inviting the top three fixed-deposit holders to a customer meet. Two customers hold exactly the same amount, and she does not want to leave either one out.
questions.schema:
FIXED_DEPOSITS(fd_no VARCHAR2(6),      -- FD number
               customer VARCHAR2(30),
               amount NUMBER(12,2))     -- principal in INR
questions.output_note: Four rows come back because FD101 and FD104 tie for third place. The order between the two tied rows is not fixed.
questions.task: List the top three fixed deposits by amount, including every deposit that ties with the third one.
questions.hint: Add WITH TIES to FETCH FIRST so equal amounts at the cut-off are kept.
questions.solution:
SELECT fd_no, customer, amount
FROM   fixed_deposits
ORDER  BY amount DESC
FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS WITH TIES;
questions.simple: Think of a race where two runners cross the line together in third place. Both get a bronze medal; nobody is sent home. The query sorts deposits from biggest to smallest and keeps the top three, plus anyone tied with number three.
questions.remember: WITH TIES = no one tied at the cut-off is left out.
questions.why: FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY stops after exactly n rows, so one of two equal amounts would be dropped at random. WITH TIES keeps extra rows whose ORDER BY value equals the last row returned. It needs an ORDER BY, and is available from Oracle 12c.
questions.tip: For a top-N report I always ask how ties should be handled, then pick ROWS ONLY or WITH TIES.

steps.say: Step one. Read the deposit number, customer and amount.
Step two. Sort from the biggest amount to the smallest.
Finally, keep the top three, plus anyone tied with the third. So we get four rows.

questions.title: Jailer 2 cities above ₹1,000
questions.scenario: Ravi in the payments team is studying Jailer 2 ticket payments made through the bank. He wants cities where successful payments add up to more than ₹1,000. Failed payments must not count.
questions.schema:
JAILER2_BOOKINGS(booking_id VARCHAR2(5),
                 city VARCHAR2(20),
                 amount NUMBER(8,2),       -- ticket payment in INR
                 pay_status VARCHAR2(10))  -- SUCCESS / FAILED
questions.output_note: Bengaluru reaches only 900 once the failed 900 payment is removed. All figures are invented sample data.
questions.task: Show each city with its number of successful bookings and total paid, only where the successful total is above ₹1,000. Biggest total first.
questions.hint: Filter rows with WHERE before grouping, and filter groups with HAVING after.
questions.solution:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS bookings, SUM(amount) AS total_paid
FROM   jailer2_bookings
WHERE  pay_status = 'SUCCESS'
GROUP  BY city
HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000
ORDER  BY total_paid DESC;
questions.simple: Imagine sorting coins into piggy banks, one per city. First you throw away the fake coins, that is WHERE. Then you count each piggy bank and keep only the ones with more than 1,000, that is HAVING. The query does exactly that with ticket payments.
questions.remember: WHERE checks rows, HAVING checks groups.
questions.why: WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so failed payments never enter the sums. HAVING runs after grouping and can test aggregates like SUM(amount), which WHERE cannot. Putting the status test in HAVING would not work, because pay_status is not a grouped column.
questions.tip: I put plain row filters in WHERE and only aggregate conditions in HAVING, which is both correct and faster.

steps.say: Step one. Keep only the successful payments. Failed ones are dropped before anything is added up.
Step two. Group the payments by city, and count and add them.
Step three. Keep only cities whose total is above one thousand rupees.
Finally, show the biggest total first. Chennai, then Hyderabad.

trend.hook: Jailer 2 is packing theatres. Which cities really paid the most? One SQL rule decides.

questions.title: Flag days the rupee hit a low
questions.scenario: Neha on the forex desk keeps a daily USD/INR rate. A higher rate means a weaker rupee. She wants each day flagged when the rate is above every earlier day, a new record low for the rupee.
questions.schema:
FX_RATES(rate_date DATE,
         usd_inr NUMBER(6,2))   -- rupees per US dollar (sample values)
questions.output_note: 19-11 only equals the earlier high, so it is not a new record. Rates are invented sample data, not real market prices.
questions.task: For every day show the rate, the highest rate on any earlier day, and Y if today beats it (otherwise N).
questions.hint: Use MAX() OVER with a frame that ends at 1 PRECEDING so today is not compared with itself.
questions.solution:
SELECT rate_date, usd_inr, prev_high,
       CASE WHEN usd_inr > prev_high THEN 'Y' ELSE 'N' END AS is_record
FROM (
  SELECT rate_date, usd_inr,
         MAX(usd_inr) OVER (ORDER BY rate_date
                            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS prev_high
  FROM   fx_rates
)
ORDER  BY rate_date;
questions.simple: Think of marking the tallest jump on a school sports chart. Each day you look only at earlier jumps; if today is higher than all of them, it is a new record. The query keeps a running highest rate of the days before, and says Y when today beats it.
questions.remember: Exclude today: frame ends at 1 PRECEDING.
questions.why: With the default frame, MAX would include the current row, so every day would be at least equal to its own high. ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING looks only at earlier days, and returns NULL on the first day. The strict > comparison means a tie with the old high is not a new record, and NULL > value falls to N.
questions.tip: For record-high or record-low flags I compare against a running MAX that stops one row before the current one.

steps.say: Step one. For each day, find the highest rate on all the days before it.
steps.to: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING

steps.say: The frame stops one row early, so today is never compared with itself.
steps.find: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING

steps.say: Step two. If today's rate is higher than that earlier high, mark it Y.
steps.find: CASE WHEN usd_inr > prev_high THEN 'Y' ELSE 'N' END AS is_record

steps.say: Finally, list the days in order. Two days set a new record.

trend.hook: The rupee keeps hitting new lows against the dollar. Can SQL spot every record day?

questions.title: Find late monthly premium payments
questions.scenario: Deepak in term-life servicing wants policies at risk of lapsing. A monthly premium paid more than 40 days after the previous payment of the same policy must be flagged.
questions.schema:
PREMIUM_PAYMENTS(policy_no VARCHAR2(6),
                 paid_on DATE)   -- date the monthly premium was received
questions.output_note: TL03's first payment has no earlier payment of its own, so it is not compared with TL02.
questions.task: Show each payment made more than 40 days after the previous payment of the same policy, with the previous date and the gap in days.
questions.hint: LAG(paid_on) needs PARTITION BY policy_no, and the filter must go in an outer query.
questions.solution:
SELECT policy_no, prev_paid, paid_on, paid_on - prev_paid AS gap_days
FROM (
  SELECT policy_no, paid_on,
         LAG(paid_on) OVER (PARTITION BY policy_no ORDER BY paid_on) AS prev_paid
  FROM   premium_payments
)
WHERE  paid_on - prev_paid > 40
ORDER  BY policy_no;
questions.simple: Think of a passbook for each policy. You look at each entry and the one just above it in the same passbook, never in someone else's. If the gap is more than 40 days, that payment was late. LAG peeks at the row above, and PARTITION BY keeps each policy in its own passbook.
questions.remember: PARTITION BY = each policy gets its own passbook.
questions.why: LAG returns the previous row in the window, and PARTITION BY restarts the window for each policy, so the first payment of TL03 gets NULL instead of TL02's date. Subtracting two DATEs gives days. Window functions cannot appear in WHERE, so the filter sits in an outer query, where NULL gaps drop out automatically.
questions.tip: Whenever I use LAG on per-customer data, I check the PARTITION BY first, because missing it silently compares different customers.

steps.say: Step one. For each payment, peek at the previous payment of the same policy.
steps.find: LAG(paid_on) OVER (PARTITION BY policy_no ORDER BY paid_on) AS prev_paid

steps.say: Step two. Subtract the dates to get the gap in days.
steps.find: SELECT policy_no, prev_paid, paid_on, paid_on - prev_paid AS gap_days

steps.say: Finally, keep only gaps over forty days. Two late payments are found.

questions.title: YoY card spend growth, gaps handled
questions.scenario: Farhan in cards analytics reports year-on-year spend growth per card variant. The RuPay Select card was paused in 2024, so its 2025 figure must not be compared with 2023.
questions.schema:
CARD_SPEND(card_variant VARCHAR2(15),
           spend_year NUMBER(4),
           total_spend NUMBER(14,2))   -- yearly spend in INR
questions.output_note: RUPAY_SELECT 2025 shows NULL because the row before it is 2023, not 2024. A plain LAG would wrongly show 50% growth.
questions.task: For each variant and year, show the previous year's spend (only if that year is exactly one year earlier) and the YoY growth percentage rounded to 2 decimals.
questions.hint: Compare LAG(spend_year) with spend_year - 1 before trusting LAG(total_spend).
questions.solution:
SELECT card_variant, spend_year, total_spend, prev_spend,
       ROUND((total_spend - prev_spend) * 100 / prev_spend, 2) AS yoy_pct
FROM (
  SELECT card_variant, spend_year, total_spend,
         CASE WHEN LAG(spend_year) OVER (PARTITION BY card_variant ORDER BY spend_year) = spend_year - 1
              THEN LAG(total_spend) OVER (PARTITION BY card_variant ORDER BY spend_year)
         END AS prev_spend
  FROM   card_spend
)
ORDER  BY card_variant, spend_year;
questions.simple: Imagine comparing your height on each birthday with last year's. If you missed a year's photo, you cannot call the jump from two years ago "one year of growth". The query checks the previous row really is last year before using it, and then works out the percentage change.
questions.remember: LAG gives the previous row, not the previous year.
questions.why: LAG returns the prior row in the partition, so a missing year makes it silently compare across two years. Checking that LAG(spend_year) = spend_year - 1 makes prev_spend NULL whenever the gap exists. Growth is (current - previous) * 100 / previous, and NULL propagates so the first year and gap years show no growth.
questions.tip: For YoY or MoM growth I verify the previous period is actually adjacent, or densify the calendar first with a partitioned outer join.

steps.say: Step one. Look at the previous row for the same card variant.
steps.find: CASE WHEN LAG(spend_year) OVER (PARTITION BY card_variant ORDER BY spend_year) = spend_year - 1

steps.say: Only if that row is exactly last year, take its spend. Otherwise it stays empty.
steps.find: THEN LAG(total_spend) OVER (PARTITION BY card_variant ORDER BY spend_year)

steps.say: Step two. Growth is this year minus last year, times a hundred, divided by last year.
Finally, Platinum shows plus twenty five, then minus ten, and the paused RuPay card shows no fake growth.

questions.title: Post late fees with WHERE CURRENT OF
questions.scenario: Suresh runs the card late-fee batch on 20-11-2026. Cards whose due date has passed and whose payment is below the minimum due get ₹500 fee, or ₹750 if the minimum due is above ₹5,000. Some payments are NULL.
questions.schema:
CARD_DUES(card_no VARCHAR2(6),
          due_date DATE,
          min_due NUMBER(10,2),    -- minimum amount due, INR
          paid NUMBER(10,2),       -- amount paid so far, NULL = nothing recorded
          late_fee NUMBER(8,2))
questions.output_note: CARD_DUES after the block. C1001 paid in full and C1004 is not due yet; C1005 counts as unpaid because NVL turns NULL into 0.
questions.task: Write an anonymous block that locks the overdue, underpaid cards and sets each late fee using UPDATE ... WHERE CURRENT OF.
questions.hint: Declare the cursor FOR UPDATE OF late_fee, then update the row the cursor is on.
questions.simple: Think of a teacher walking down a queue of students holding a red pen. She stops at each student who did not finish homework and writes a mark right there, on that student's page. The cursor is the teacher walking the queue, and WHERE CURRENT OF means "write on the page I am standing at".
questions.remember: WHERE CURRENT OF = update the row I am on.
questions.why: FOR UPDATE OF locks every selected row when the cursor opens, so no other session can change the dues while fees are posted. WHERE CURRENT OF updates the exact row just fetched using its ROWID, so no second key lookup is needed. COMMIT goes after the loop, because committing inside a FOR UPDATE loop releases the locks and the next fetch fails with ORA-01002.
questions.tip: When I must read and update the same rows in a loop, I lock them with FOR UPDATE and update with WHERE CURRENT OF, then commit once at the end.

steps.say: Step one. The cursor picks cards that are overdue and paid less than the minimum. NULL payments count as zero.
FOR UPDATE locks those rows, so nobody else can change them meanwhile.
Step two. For each locked row, set the fee: five hundred, or seven fifty for bigger dues.
steps.to: SET    late_fee = CASE WHEN r.min_due <= 5000 THEN 500 ELSE 750 END

steps.say: WHERE CURRENT OF updates exactly the row the cursor is standing on.
Finally, commit once after the loop. Three cards get a late fee.

questions.title: Keep NACH batch running past errors
questions.scenario: Anjali runs the NACH auto-debit batch. One bad mandate must not stop the rest: debits that fail for low balance or an unknown account should be logged in NACH_ERRORS with the error code.
questions.schema:
ACCOUNTS(account_no VARCHAR2(6),
         balance NUMBER(12,2) CONSTRAINT chk_bal CHECK (balance >= 0))
MANDATE_REQUESTS(req_id NUMBER, account_no VARCHAR2(6), amount NUMBER(12,2))
NACH_ERRORS(req_id NUMBER, err_code NUMBER)   -- empty before the run
questions.output_note: NACH_ERRORS after the run. Request 2 broke the CHECK constraint and request 3 found no account; requests 1 and 4 still went through, leaving SB101 = 7000 and SB103 = 0.
questions.task: Write a block that debits every mandate in req_id order, logs any failure with its SQLCODE into NACH_ERRORS, and carries on with the next request.
questions.hint: Wrap the work for each row in its own BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END inside the loop.
questions.simple: Think of a postman delivering letters down a street. If one house has no letterbox, he writes it in his notebook and walks on to the next house; he does not go home. The inner BEGIN and EXCEPTION is that notebook: each failed debit is noted, and the loop keeps going.
questions.remember: Inner BEGIN-EXCEPTION-END = one bad row, not a dead batch.
questions.why: Without the inner block, the first exception would leave the loop and end the whole batch. A failed UPDATE is rolled back only at statement level, so earlier successful debits stay in place. SQLCODE cannot be used directly inside a SQL statement, so it is first copied into a PL/SQL variable, and an UPDATE that matches no row raises nothing, hence the SQL%ROWCOUNT check.
questions.tip: In batch jobs I handle exceptions per row and log them, so one bad record never blocks thousands of good ones.

steps.say: Step one. Loop through the mandates in order.
steps.find: FOR r IN (SELECT req_id, account_no, amount
steps.to: FROM   mandate_requests ORDER BY req_id) LOOP

steps.say: Step two. Debit the account. A balance below zero breaks the check rule and raises an error.
If no account was found, raise our own error, minus two zero zero zero one.
Step three. Any error is caught right here, logged with its code, and the loop moves on.
steps.to: INSERT INTO nach_errors (req_id, err_code) VALUES (r.req_id, v_code);

steps.say: Finally, two debits succeed and two errors are logged.

questions.title: Build address validity ranges
questions.scenario: Kavitha in KYC must show which city each customer lived in, and from when to when. The log also has re-KYC rows where the city did not change; these must not start a new period.
questions.schema:
ADDRESS_LOG(cust_id VARCHAR2(4),
            changed_on DATE,       -- date the address was recorded
            city VARCHAR2(20))
questions.output_note: NULL valid_to means the address is still current. C1 moving back to Pune correctly opens a second Pune period.
questions.task: Return one row per real address period with valid_from and valid_to (the day before the next real change, NULL if current).
questions.hint: First keep rows where the city differs from the previous row (LAG), then use LEAD on what is left.
questions.solution:
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT cust_id, changed_on, city,
         LAG(city) OVER (PARTITION BY cust_id ORDER BY changed_on) AS prev_city
  FROM   address_log
)
SELECT cust_id, city,
       changed_on AS valid_from,
       LEAD(changed_on) OVER (PARTITION BY cust_id ORDER BY changed_on) - 1 AS valid_to
FROM   flagged
WHERE  prev_city IS NULL OR prev_city <> city
ORDER  BY cust_id, valid_from;
questions.simple: Imagine a school register of where each child sits. If the teacher writes the same seat again, nothing really changed, so you cross it out. Then each remaining entry lasts until the day before the next one. The query removes repeat entries with LAG and finds the end date with LEAD.
questions.remember: LAG removes repeats, LEAD closes the period.
questions.why: LAG compares each row with the previous one for the same customer, so unchanged re-KYC rows can be filtered out. Window functions in the outer SELECT run after its WHERE, so LEAD sees only the real change rows and returns the next real change date. Subtracting 1 makes periods non-overlapping, and LEAD returns NULL for the current period.
questions.tip: To build SCD Type 2 history from a raw log I drop no-change rows with LAG first, then derive end dates with LEAD.

steps.say: Step one. Next to each row, put the previous city of the same customer.
steps.find: LAG(city) OVER (PARTITION BY cust_id ORDER BY changed_on) AS prev_city

steps.say: Step two. Keep only real changes: the first row, or a row where the city is different.
steps.find: WHERE  prev_city IS NULL OR prev_city <> city

steps.say: Step three. On those rows, the next change date minus one day ends the period.
steps.find: LEAD(changed_on) OVER (PARTITION BY cust_id ORDER BY changed_on) - 1 AS valid_to

steps.say: Finally, the current address has no end date. Customer C1 gets three periods, C2 just one.

questions.title: First and last drop per rider
questions.scenario: Sana runs rider operations for a food delivery app in Bengaluru. She wants each rider's first and last delivery time on 23 November, plus how many orders they dropped.
questions.schema:
RIDER_ORDERS(order_id VARCHAR2(5),
             rider_id VARCHAR2(5),
             delivered_at DATE)   -- date and time of drop
questions.output_note: R3 made only one drop, so first and last are the same time.
questions.task: For each rider, show the number of orders, the earliest delivered_at and the latest delivered_at.
questions.hint: MIN and MAX work on dates too: earliest is MIN, latest is MAX.
questions.solution:
SELECT rider_id,
       COUNT(*)          AS orders,
       MIN(delivered_at) AS first_drop,
       MAX(delivered_at) AS last_drop
FROM   rider_orders
GROUP  BY rider_id
ORDER  BY rider_id;
questions.simple: Think of a school attendance register with the time each child arrived. The earliest time is who came first, the latest is who came last. GROUP BY makes one pile per rider, and MIN and MAX pick the earliest and latest time in each pile.
questions.remember: MIN = earliest, MAX = latest, even for dates.
questions.why: GROUP BY rider_id collapses all orders of a rider into one row. MIN and MAX on a DATE column compare chronologically, including the time part. COUNT(*) counts rows in each group.
questions.tip: MIN and MAX work on numbers, dates and strings, so I use them for first and last events per group.

steps.say: Step one. Make one group per rider.
Step two. Count the orders in each group.
Step three. MIN gives the earliest drop time, MAX gives the latest.

questions.title: Opening-day bookings by city
questions.scenario: Yeh Prem Mol Liya opens in theatres on 27 November. Rohit at a ticket booking app has advance bookings for the first few days and wants opening-day tickets next to total tickets per city.
questions.schema:
ADVANCE_BOOKINGS(city VARCHAR2(20),
                 show_date DATE,     -- day of the show
                 tickets NUMBER)     -- tickets booked so far
questions.output_note: Sample data only. Delhi has the most tickets overall, but Mumbai leads on opening day.
questions.task: Per city, show opening-day (27-11-2026) tickets and total advance tickets, highest opening day first.
questions.hint: Put a CASE inside SUM so only opening-day rows add their tickets.

SELECT city,

FROM   advance_bookings

questions.simple: Imagine counting money in two piggy banks at once: one only for Friday coins, one for all coins. For every row, the CASE asks: is this the opening day? If yes, add the tickets to the first pile, otherwise add zero. The second SUM adds everything.
questions.remember: SUM(CASE ...) = count only the rows you choose.
questions.why: Conditional aggregation evaluates the CASE per row before summing, so one pass over the table gives several totals. ELSE 0 keeps the sum at 0 instead of NULL for a city with no opening-day row. This is the classic manual pivot.
questions.tip: I use SUM with CASE to build several filtered totals side by side in a single GROUP BY.

steps.say: Step one. One row per city.
Step two. Add tickets only when the show is on opening day, otherwise add zero.
steps.to: THEN tickets ELSE 0 END) AS day1_tickets

steps.say: Step three. A plain SUM gives all advance tickets.

questions.title: Silver loans pushed over LTV
questions.scenario: Silver prices have fallen sharply this month. Priya in the bank's silver loan team must find loans that were within the 75% LTV limit on 10 November but are above it at the 23 November rate.
questions.schema:
SILVER_LOANS(loan_id VARCHAR2(4), cust_name VARCHAR2(20),
             silver_grams NUMBER,   -- pledged silver
             outstanding NUMBER)    -- rupees due
SILVER_RATES(rate_date DATE, rate_per_kg NUMBER)
questions.output_note: Invented rates, not real prices. L3 is excluded because it was already above 75% before the fall.
questions.task: LTV % = outstanding * 100 / (silver_grams / 1000 * rate_per_kg). List loans with LTV <= 75 on 10-11-2026 and > 75 on 23-11-2026, highest current LTV first.
questions.hint: Join SILVER_RATES twice with two aliases, one for each date.
questions.solution:
SELECT l.loan_id, l.cust_name,
       ROUND(l.outstanding * 100 / (l.silver_grams / 1000 * b.rate_per_kg), 1) AS ltv_before,
       ROUND(l.outstanding * 100 / (l.silver_grams / 1000 * n.rate_per_kg), 1) AS ltv_now
FROM   silver_loans l
CROSS  JOIN silver_rates b
CROSS  JOIN silver_rates n
WHERE  b.rate_date = DATE '2026-11-10'
AND    n.rate_date = DATE '2026-11-23'
AND    l.outstanding * 100 / (l.silver_grams / 1000 * b.rate_per_kg) <= 75
AND    l.outstanding * 100 / (l.silver_grams / 1000 * n.rate_per_kg) > 75
ORDER  BY ltv_now DESC;
questions.simple: Imagine checking a child's height against a door mark twice: last month and today. You need both readings side by side. The query opens the price list twice, once for the old date and once for today, so every loan sees both prices and can be compared.
questions.remember: Need two rows of one table? Join it twice.
questions.why: Each alias of SILVER_RATES is filtered to one date, so each CROSS JOIN adds exactly one row and one price column per loan. Both LTVs are then on the same row and can be compared in WHERE. The WHERE repeats the expressions because column aliases are not visible there.
questions.tip: To compare a value on two dates I self-join the rate table with two aliases instead of running two queries.

steps.say: Step one. Bring in the rate table twice: b for before, n for now.
Step two. Pin b to tenth November and n to twenty-third November.
Step three. Keep loans that were safe before, but are above seventy-five percent now.
Finally, Gopal and Meena crossed the limit. Farida was already over it, so she is not new.
