questions.title: Plan revenue share per circle
questions.scenario: Aditya, an analyst at a telecom operator, has monthly revenue for each recharge plan in each circle. Management wants each plan's share within its own circle, not of the whole country.
questions.schema:
PLAN_REVENUE(circle VARCHAR2(20),
             plan_name VARCHAR2(30),
             revenue_lakh NUMBER)   -- revenue in lakh rupees
questions.output_note: Every circle's shares add up to 100. Without PARTITION BY, Kerala's 27 would be only about 11% of the whole table.
questions.task: Show each plan's revenue and its percentage share of its circle's total revenue, rounded to 1 decimal, sorted by circle then share descending.
questions.hint: RATIO_TO_REPORT(x) OVER (PARTITION BY circle) returns x divided by the circle total.
questions.solution:
SELECT circle, plan_name, revenue_lakh,
       ROUND(100 * RATIO_TO_REPORT(revenue_lakh)
                   OVER (PARTITION BY circle), 1) AS share_pct
FROM   plan_revenue
ORDER  BY circle, share_pct DESC;
questions.simple: Think of a class pizza party where each table shares its own pizza. Your slice is measured against your table's pizza, not every pizza in the hall. PARTITION BY circle makes one pizza per circle, and RATIO_TO_REPORT tells each plan what part of that pizza it ate.
questions.remember: RATIO_TO_REPORT = my share of my group's total.
questions.why: RATIO_TO_REPORT is an analytic function equal to value / SUM(value) OVER the same partition. PARTITION BY circle resets the denominator for each circle while keeping every detail row. The portable equivalent is revenue_lakh / SUM(revenue_lakh) OVER (PARTITION BY circle).
questions.tip: For percent-of-total I use RATIO_TO_REPORT or value / SUM() OVER, and I check the partition so shares add to 100 per group.

steps.say: Step one. RATIO_TO_REPORT divides each plan's revenue by a total.
Step two. PARTITION BY circle makes that total the circle's own revenue.
Finally, sort by circle and biggest share. Kerala's unlimited plan holds seventy-five percent.

questions.title: Median items per order
questions.scenario: Kunal at an online shopping app stores a summary instead of raw orders: how many orders had 1 item, 2 items, and so on. He needs the median number of items per order.
questions.schema:
ITEMS_PER_ORDER(items NUMBER,         -- items in one order
                order_count NUMBER)   -- orders with that many items
questions.output_note: 12 orders in total, so the median is the average of the 6th order (2 items) and the 7th order (3 items).
questions.task: Without expanding the rows, return the median number of items per order, rounded to 1 decimal.
questions.hint: A running SUM of order_count tells you which items value covers the middle position(s).
questions.solution:
WITH c AS (
  SELECT items, order_count,
         SUM(order_count) OVER (ORDER BY items) AS cum_cnt,
         SUM(order_count) OVER ()               AS total_cnt
  FROM   items_per_order
)
SELECT ROUND(AVG(items), 1) AS median_items
FROM   c
WHERE  cum_cnt >= total_cnt / 2
AND    cum_cnt - order_count <= total_cnt / 2;
questions.simple: Imagine 12 children standing in a line by height, but you only know how many are of each height. You count along the groups until you reach the middle two children. The query keeps a running count, finds the groups holding the middle positions, and averages them.
questions.remember: Running count finds the middle; AVG handles two middles.
questions.why: cum_cnt is the last position covered by each items value and cum_cnt - order_count is the position just before it. With total/2 as real division, the WHERE keeps one row for an odd total and the one or two rows holding positions N/2 and N/2+1 for an even total. AVG then returns the median without expanding 12 rows.
questions.tip: For a median over a frequency table I use a running SUM of counts instead of exploding rows, which scales to millions of orders.

steps.say: Step one. A running total of orders: the last position each item count reaches.
steps.find: SUM(order_count) OVER (ORDER BY items) AS cum_cnt

steps.say: Step two. The grand total of orders, here twelve.
Step three. Keep groups that cover the middle positions, six and seven.
Finally, average them: two and three give a median of two point five.

questions.title: Salary cap trigger blocks update
questions.scenario: Payroll has a rule: no raise above 50% in one go. Deepak in HR runs one UPDATE giving the IT team 10%, but a typo gives Kiran 60%.
questions.schema:
EMPLOYEES(emp_id VARCHAR2(4), name VARCHAR2(20),
          dept VARCHAR2(10), salary NUMBER)
questions.output_note: The UPDATE fails with ORA-20001: Raise above 50% for E3. Oracle rolls back the whole statement, so even E1 and E2 keep their old salaries.
questions.task: After the trigger is created and the UPDATE runs, what does EMPLOYEES contain, and what error appears?
questions.hint: An error in a row trigger undoes the entire triggering statement, not only that row.
questions.simple: Think of a class photo: if one child blinks, the teacher throws away the whole photo and nobody gets a copy. The trigger checks each salary change. When it finds Kiran's 60% raise it raises an error, and Oracle cancels the entire UPDATE, so nobody's salary changes.
questions.remember: One row fails, the whole statement is undone.
questions.why: A BEFORE ROW trigger fires for each updated row and can compare :OLD and :NEW values. RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR raises a user-defined ORA-20000 to ORA-20999 error. Oracle uses statement-level atomicity, so all rows changed by that UPDATE are rolled back, while earlier work in the transaction stays.
questions.tip: I enforce row rules with RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR in a BEFORE ROW trigger and rely on statement-level rollback to keep data consistent.

steps.say: Step one. The trigger fires before every salary update, once per row.
steps.find: BEFORE UPDATE OF salary ON employees

steps.say: Step two. If the new salary is more than one and a half times the old one, raise an error.
Step three. The update gives Kiran sixty percent by mistake.
steps.find: SET    salary = CASE emp_id WHEN 'E3' THEN salary * 1.6

steps.say: Finally, Kiran's row fails, so Oracle undoes the whole update. Ravi and Divya get nothing either.

questions.title: Reorder medicines per pharmacy store
questions.scenario: A pharmacy chain in Chennai reorders medicines that fall below their reorder level. Retail stores order up to twice the level; hospital stores order up to three times.
questions.schema:
STORES(store_id VARCHAR2(3), store_type VARCHAR2(10))
PHARMACY_STOCK(store_id VARCHAR2(3), medicine VARCHAR2(20),
               qty NUMBER, reorder_level NUMBER)
REORDER_REQ(store_id VARCHAR2(3), medicine VARCHAR2(20), order_qty NUMBER)
questions.output_note: REORDER_REQ after the block, shown ordered by store and medicine. S1 ORS is not reordered because 25 is not below 25.
questions.task: Run the block. What rows end up in REORDER_REQ?
questions.hint: The cursor is reopened for every store with that store's id and factor.
questions.simple: Think of a shopkeeper with one shopping-list form that has two blanks: which shop, and how much extra to buy. For each shop he fills the blanks and gets that shop's list. The cursor is the form, and the parameters are the blanks filled for each store.
questions.remember: Parameterized cursor = one query, new inputs each loop.
questions.why: Cursor parameters are bound when the cursor opens, so the same cursor runs once per store with a different p_store and p_factor. A cursor FOR loop opens, fetches and closes it automatically each time. In production a single INSERT ... SELECT joined to STORES would do this set-based, which is faster.
questions.tip: I use parameterized cursors to reuse one query with different inputs, but I prefer a single set-based INSERT SELECT when no row-by-row logic is needed.

steps.say: Step one. The cursor takes a store and a factor, and finds medicines below their reorder level.
steps.find: CURSOR c_low (p_store VARCHAR2, p_factor NUMBER) IS

steps.say: Step two. Loop through stores. Hospitals get factor three, others factor two.
steps.find: FOR s IN (SELECT store_id, store_type FROM stores ORDER BY store_id) LOOP
steps.to: v_factor := CASE s.store_type WHEN 'HOSPITAL' THEN 3 ELSE 2 END;

steps.say: Step three. Open the cursor for this store and insert each reorder line.
steps.find: FOR m IN c_low(s.store_id, v_factor) LOOP
steps.to: INSERT INTO reorder_req VALUES (s.store_id, m.medicine, m.order_qty);

steps.say: Finally, three lines are saved. ORS is exactly at its level, so it is not reordered.

questions.title: Longest winning streak per team
questions.scenario: Ishaan builds stats for a T20 league app. For each team he must show its longest run of consecutive wins and when that run started and ended.
questions.schema:
MATCH_RESULTS(team VARCHAR2(5),
              match_date DATE,
              result CHAR(1))   -- W = won, L = lost
questions.output_note: PUN's first win on 01-04 is a separate streak of 1, broken by the loss on 04-04.
questions.task: For each team, return the longest streak of consecutive wins with its first and last match date. Show ties if a team has two equal longest streaks.
questions.hint: Subtract a ROW_NUMBER per team and result from a ROW_NUMBER per team: the difference is constant inside a streak.
questions.solution:
WITH w AS (
  SELECT team, match_date, result,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY team ORDER BY match_date)
       - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY team, result ORDER BY match_date) AS grp
  FROM   match_results
), s AS (
  SELECT team, grp, COUNT(*) AS streak,
         MIN(match_date) AS from_date, MAX(match_date) AS to_date
  FROM   w
  WHERE  result = 'W'
  GROUP  BY team, grp
)
SELECT team, streak, from_date, to_date
FROM  (SELECT s.*, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY team ORDER BY streak DESC) AS rk
       FROM   s)
WHERE  rk = 1
ORDER  BY team;
questions.simple: Imagine two counters for a team: one counts every match, the other counts only wins. While the team keeps winning, both go up together, so the gap between them stays the same. A loss changes the gap. Same gap means same streak, so we group by it and count.
questions.remember: Same gap between two counters = same streak.
questions.why: Within a run of consecutive W rows both ROW_NUMBERs increase by 1, so their difference stays constant and labels the island. Grouping W rows by team and grp gives each streak's length and dates. RANK in the outer query keeps the longest streak per team, including ties.
questions.tip: For consecutive-run problems I use the ROW_NUMBER difference trick to label islands, then aggregate and rank them.

steps.say: Step one. Two counters: every match, and matches with the same result. Their difference labels each streak.
steps.find: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY team ORDER BY match_date)
steps.to: - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY team, result ORDER BY match_date) AS grp

steps.say: Step two. Keep only wins and group by that label to get each streak's length and dates.
Step three. Rank streaks per team, longest first.
steps.find: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY team ORDER BY streak DESC) AS rk

steps.say: Finally, keep rank one. Pune's best run is three wins, Kochi's is two.

questions.title: Trips and unique drivers per city
questions.scenario: A ride-hailing app wants a city report. For each city it needs the number of trips and the number of different drivers who did them.
questions.schema:
TRIPS(trip_id VARCHAR2(5),   -- trip id
      city VARCHAR2(20),     -- pickup city
      driver_id VARCHAR2(5), -- driver who did the trip
      fare NUMBER)           -- fare in rupees
questions.output_note: Driver D1 did two Bengaluru trips but is counted once in drivers.
questions.task: Show each city with its total trips and its number of unique drivers, ordered by city.
questions.hint: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts different values.
questions.solution:
SELECT city,
       COUNT(*)                  AS trips,
       COUNT(DISTINCT driver_id) AS drivers
FROM   trips
GROUP  BY city
ORDER  BY city;
questions.simple: Think of a school register for a bus. Seven rides happened, but some children rode twice. COUNT(*) counts every ride, while COUNT DISTINCT counts each child only once. Here we do that for each city.
questions.remember: COUNT DISTINCT = count each person only once.
questions.why: COUNT(*) counts every row in the group, while COUNT(DISTINCT driver_id) removes duplicate driver ids before counting. NULL driver ids would be ignored by COUNT DISTINCT. Both run per city because of GROUP BY.
questions.tip: I use COUNT(DISTINCT) for unique customers or drivers, and remember it skips NULL values.

steps.say: Step one. Group the trips by city.
Step two. COUNT star counts every trip in the city.
Step three. COUNT DISTINCT counts each driver only once.
Finally, Bengaluru has three trips but only two drivers, because D1 drove twice.

questions.title: Students with their course names
questions.scenario: An ed-tech platform in Noida lists each student with the course they joined. Some students have no course yet, and one has a course id that does not exist.
questions.schema:
STUDENTS(student_id VARCHAR2(3), name VARCHAR2(20),
         course_id VARCHAR2(3))     -- NULL if not enrolled
COURSES(course_id VARCHAR2(3), course_name VARCHAR2(20))
questions.output_note: Kabir (NULL course) and Meera (C9 not in COURSES) disappear. Data Science has no students, so it is not shown either.
questions.task: Run the query. Which rows come back, and why do two students go missing?
questions.hint: An INNER JOIN keeps only rows that find a match on both sides.
questions.solution:
SELECT s.name, c.course_name
FROM   students s
JOIN   courses  c
       ON c.course_id = s.course_id
ORDER  BY s.name;
questions.simple: Imagine matching socks from two baskets. Only socks that find a partner go in the drawer; lonely socks stay out. An INNER JOIN keeps only students whose course id finds a partner in the courses list.
questions.remember: INNER JOIN = only pairs that match, nobody alone.
questions.why: JOIN without a keyword is an INNER JOIN, so a student row survives only when the ON condition is true. NULL = 'C1' is unknown, not true, so Kabir is dropped, and C9 has no partner. A LEFT JOIN would keep all four students with NULL course names.
questions.tip: When rows vanish after a join, I first check for NULL keys and missing master rows, then decide if a LEFT JOIN is needed.

steps.say: Step one. Join students to courses on the course id.
Step two. Only matching pairs survive. Kabir has no course, and Meera's course C9 does not exist.
Finally, only Aarav and Diya come back, sorted by name.

questions.title: Languages above the average language total
questions.scenario: 2026 is being called a record year for Indian cinema. A film trade dashboard wants the languages whose 2026 total beats the average language total. All figures are invented sample data.
questions.schema:
FILM_COLLECTIONS(film VARCHAR2(30),
                 language VARCHAR2(15),
                 release_year NUMBER,
                 net_cr NUMBER)   -- net collection in crore rupees (sample)
questions.output_note: 2026 totals: Hindi 800, Telugu 540, Tamil 310, Malayalam 70. Average = 1720 / 4 = 430. The 2025 film is ignored on both sides.
questions.task: For 2026 only, show languages whose total net collection is above the average language total, biggest first.
questions.hint: Compute the average in a subquery inside HAVING: total of 2026 divided by number of languages.
questions.solution:
SELECT language, SUM(net_cr) AS total_net_cr
FROM   film_collections
WHERE  release_year = 2026
GROUP  BY language
HAVING SUM(net_cr) > (SELECT SUM(net_cr) / COUNT(DISTINCT language)
                      FROM   film_collections
                      WHERE  release_year = 2026)
ORDER  BY total_net_cr DESC;
questions.simple: Think of four classes collecting money for a school fair. First you find what an average class collected. Then you clap only for classes that beat that average. The subquery finds the average, and HAVING keeps the languages that beat it.
questions.remember: HAVING filters groups; a subquery can give the bar.
questions.why: WHERE removes 2025 rows before grouping, and HAVING filters the language groups after SUM is computed. The scalar subquery returns a single number, 430, which each group total is compared with. The subquery needs its own year filter, or Old Glory would raise the average.
questions.tip: I filter rows in WHERE and groups in HAVING, and I make sure any subquery used as a threshold has the same filters.

steps.say: Step one. Keep only 2026 films and add up collections per language.
Step two. The subquery finds the average language total, which is four hundred thirty crore.
Finally, only Hindi and Telugu beat the average, shown biggest first.
