questions.title: Two worst delays per airport
questions.scenario: An airline ops team wants the two biggest departure delays at each airport today. If two flights tie, both must be shown.
questions.schema:
FLIGHT_DELAYS(flight_no VARCHAR2(6),
              airport VARCHAR2(3),  -- departure airport code
              delay_min NUMBER)     -- delay in minutes
questions.output_note: DEL returns three flights because AI101 and UK303 tie at 45 minutes.
questions.task: For each airport, return flights ranked 1 or 2 by delay (largest first), keeping ties.
questions.hint: RANK gives tied rows the same number; filter on it in an outer query.
questions.solution:
SELECT airport, flight_no, delay_min, rnk
FROM  (SELECT airport, flight_no, delay_min,
              RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY airport
                           ORDER BY delay_min DESC) AS rnk
       FROM   flight_delays)
WHERE  rnk <= 2
ORDER  BY airport, rnk, flight_no;
questions.simple: Think of a race where two runners cross the line together. Both get the silver medal. RANK works the same way: tied flights get the same number, so both appear in the top two.
questions.remember: RANK shares places on a tie; ROW_NUMBER never does.
questions.why: RANK restarts for every airport because of PARTITION BY, and equal delays get the same rank. A window function cannot be used directly in WHERE, so the filter goes in an outer query. ROW_NUMBER would randomly drop one of the tied 45-minute flights.
questions.tip: For top-N per group I choose RANK, DENSE_RANK or ROW_NUMBER based on how the business wants ties handled.

steps.say: Step one. Rank flights inside each airport, biggest delay first.
steps.to: ORDER BY delay_min DESC) AS rnk

steps.say: Step two. Keep ranks one and two in the outer query.
Finally, Delhi shows three flights, because two of them tie at forty five minutes.

questions.title: Weekly open and close for crude
questions.scenario: Crude oil prices have been sliding. A bank's treasury desk tracks daily Brent prices for its oil-importer clients and wants weekly open, high, low and close. Prices are invented sample data.
questions.schema:
CRUDE_PRICES(price_date DATE,
             brent_usd NUMBER(6,2))  -- sample closing price per barrel
questions.output_note: Rows are stored out of date order, so open and close must come from ORDER BY price_date, not from row order. Week 2's high (98.40) is mid-week.
questions.task: For each ISO week, show open (first date's price), high, low, close (last date's price) and % change from open to close, rounded to 2 decimals.
questions.hint: MIN(x) KEEP (DENSE_RANK FIRST ORDER BY d) picks x from the earliest date in the group.
questions.solution:
SELECT week_start, open_px, high_px, low_px, close_px,
       ROUND((close_px - open_px) / open_px * 100, 2) AS pct_change
FROM  (SELECT TRUNC(price_date, 'IW') AS week_start,
              MIN(brent_usd) KEEP (DENSE_RANK FIRST ORDER BY price_date) AS open_px,
              MAX(brent_usd) AS high_px,
              MIN(brent_usd) AS low_px,
              MAX(brent_usd) KEEP (DENSE_RANK LAST ORDER BY price_date) AS close_px
       FROM   crude_prices
       GROUP  BY TRUNC(price_date, 'IW'))
ORDER  BY week_start;
questions.simple: Think of a weekly diary of a petrol price board. Monday's number is the open, Friday's is the close, and the biggest and smallest numbers are the high and low. KEEP FIRST and KEEP LAST read the first and last page of each week, even if the pages were shuffled.
questions.remember: KEEP FIRST/LAST = value from the earliest or latest row.
questions.why: TRUNC(date, 'IW') maps every date to the Monday of its ISO week, which becomes the group. KEEP (DENSE_RANK FIRST/LAST ORDER BY price_date) returns the price from the earliest or latest date in one pass, without a self-join or window function. The MIN or MAX in front only breaks ties if two rows share the same date.
questions.tip: For open-close style reports I use KEEP DENSE_RANK FIRST and LAST, which avoids joining the table back to itself.

steps.say: Step one. Group every date into its week, starting Monday.
Step two. KEEP FIRST takes the price from the earliest date. That is the weekly open.
steps.find: MIN(brent_usd) KEEP (DENSE_RANK FIRST ORDER BY price_date) AS open_px,

steps.say: Step three. MAX and MIN give the high and low. KEEP LAST takes the closing price.
steps.to: MAX(brent_usd) KEEP (DENSE_RANK LAST ORDER BY price_date) AS close_px

steps.say: Finally, compute the percent change. Both sample weeks closed lower than they opened.

trend.hook: Crude oil keeps sliding. How does a bank desk build weekly candles in one SQL query?

questions.title: How many users posted how often
questions.scenario: A short-video app wants a November 2026 histogram: how many users made 0 posts, 1 post, 2 posts and so on. Users who did not post in November must land in the 0 bucket.
questions.schema:
USERS(user_id VARCHAR2(3), city VARCHAR2(15))
POSTS(post_id VARCHAR2(3),
      user_id VARCHAR2(3),
      post_date DATE)
questions.output_note: U4 only posted in October and U5 never posted, so both fall in the 0 bucket. Putting the date filter in WHERE would drop them.
questions.task: Return each post count (posts in November 2026) and how many users have that count, including users with zero posts.
questions.hint: LEFT JOIN with the date filter inside ON, count p.post_id per user, then group by that count.
questions.solution:
SELECT post_count, COUNT(*) AS num_users
FROM  (SELECT u.user_id, COUNT(p.post_id) AS post_count
       FROM   users u
       LEFT JOIN posts p
              ON  p.user_id = u.user_id
              AND p.post_date >= DATE '2026-11-01'
              AND p.post_date <  DATE '2026-12-01'
       GROUP  BY u.user_id)
GROUP  BY post_count
ORDER  BY post_count;
questions.simple: Think of a class teacher counting how many children read 0, 1, 2 or 3 books this month. First she counts books per child, even children who read none. Then she counts how many children are in each pile. The inner query counts per user, the outer query counts the piles.
questions.remember: Histogram = count per user, then count the counts.
questions.why: The LEFT JOIN keeps every user, and the date filter in ON only limits which posts match, so U4 and U5 get NULL post columns. COUNT(p.post_id) ignores those NULLs and returns 0, while COUNT(*) would wrongly return 1. The outer GROUP BY then aggregates a second time on the computed count.
questions.tip: For histograms I aggregate twice and use a LEFT JOIN with the filter in ON so the zero bucket is not lost.

steps.say: Step one. Keep every user, and match only their November posts.
Step two. Count posts per user. COUNT of post id gives zero when nothing matched.
Step three. Now group by that count, and count users in each bucket.
Finally, two users made zero posts, and one user each made one, two and three posts.

questions.title: Total nights per hotel in PL/SQL
questions.scenario: A hotel booking site sums nights per hotel in memory and writes a summary with a sequence number. Bookings arrive in booking order, not hotel order.
questions.schema:
HOTEL_BOOKINGS(booking_id VARCHAR2(3), hotel VARCHAR2(20), nights NUMBER)
HOTEL_NIGHTS(seq NUMBER,           -- order the row was written
             hotel VARCHAR2(20), total_nights NUMBER)
questions.output_note: HOTEL_NIGHTS after the block. Ooty was added to the array first, but FIRST/NEXT walk a VARCHAR2-indexed array in key sort order, so Goa gets seq 1.
questions.task: Run the block. What rows end up in HOTEL_NIGHTS, and in what seq order?
questions.hint: A string-indexed associative array is always kept sorted by its key.
questions.simple: Think of a phone contact list. You can save Ooty first and Goa later, but the list always shows names in A to Z order. A string-keyed associative array behaves like that contact list. When we walk it from FIRST to NEXT, Goa comes before Jaipur and Ooty.
questions.remember: String-keyed array = always sorted, like a contact list.
questions.why: An associative array indexed by VARCHAR2 stores elements sorted by key (using the session's NLS sort), not by insertion order. EXISTS avoids a NO_DATA_FOUND when reading a key for the first time. FIRST and NEXT return keys, so the WHILE loop stops when NEXT returns NULL after the last key.
questions.tip: I use string-keyed associative arrays as in-memory lookups and remember that FIRST/NEXT iterate in key order, not load order.

steps.say: Step one. Declare an array indexed by hotel name.
steps.find: TYPE t_nights IS TABLE OF NUMBER INDEX BY VARCHAR2(20);

steps.say: Step two. For each booking, add nights to that hotel, or start a new entry.
Step three. Walk the array from FIRST to NEXT and insert each total with a sequence.
Finally, Goa gets sequence one, because string keys come back in alphabetical order.

questions.title: Overdue EMI alert per loan
questions.scenario: A lender's collection job writes one alert per loan by reading its overdue EMI with SELECT INTO. Some loans have no overdue EMI and one has two.
questions.schema:
LOANS(loan_id VARCHAR2(3), city VARCHAR2(15))
EMI_SCHEDULE(loan_id VARCHAR2(3), emi_no NUMBER,
             status VARCHAR2(10))   -- PAID / OVERDUE
LOAN_ALERTS(loan_id VARCHAR2(3), msg VARCHAR2(40))
questions.output_note: LOAN_ALERTS after the block. Each loan has its own BEGIN-EXCEPTION block, so the errors for L2 and L3 are handled and the loop continues.
questions.task: Run the block. What rows end up in LOAN_ALERTS?
questions.hint: SELECT INTO must return exactly one row; zero or many rows raise different exceptions.
questions.simple: Think of asking a shopkeeper for 'the red pen'. If he has none, that is one problem; if he has two, he does not know which to give you. SELECT INTO is like that: it wants exactly one row. The block catches both problems for each loan and writes a friendly message instead of crashing.
questions.remember: SELECT INTO wants one row: zero or two is an error.
questions.why: SELECT INTO raises NO_DATA_FOUND for zero rows and TOO_MANY_ROWS (ORA-01422) for more than one. Wrapping the statement in an inner BEGIN-EXCEPTION-END per loop iteration handles the error locally, so the outer loop keeps going. Without the inner block, L2 would stop the whole job and nothing after it would run.
questions.tip: Around every SELECT INTO I handle NO_DATA_FOUND and TOO_MANY_ROWS explicitly, usually inside a per-row block in batch jobs.

steps.say: Step one. For each loan, read its overdue EMI with SELECT INTO.
Step two. Loan L1 has exactly one overdue EMI, so the normal alert is written.
steps.find: INSERT INTO loan_alerts VALUES (l.loan_id, 'Overdue EMI ' || v_emi);

steps.say: Step three. No row raises NO DATA FOUND. Two rows raise TOO MANY ROWS. Both are caught here.
steps.to: INSERT INTO loan_alerts VALUES (l.loan_id, 'Multiple overdue EMIs');

steps.say: Finally, every loan gets one alert, because each error was handled inside the loop.

questions.title: Power complaints by priority
questions.scenario: A power distribution company in Gujarat logs customer complaints with a priority. The night-shift team must see HIGH first, then MEDIUM, then LOW, oldest first within each.
questions.schema:
COMPLAINTS(complaint_id VARCHAR2(3),
           city         VARCHAR2(15),
           priority     VARCHAR2(6),   -- HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW
           logged_on    DATE)
questions.output_note: A plain ORDER BY priority would sort alphabetically: HIGH, LOW, MEDIUM.
questions.task: List complaint_id, city and priority with HIGH first, then MEDIUM, then LOW; inside each priority, oldest complaint first.
questions.hint: Turn each priority word into a number inside ORDER BY.
questions.solution:
SELECT complaint_id, city, priority
FROM   complaints
ORDER  BY CASE priority WHEN 'HIGH'   THEN 1
                        WHEN 'MEDIUM' THEN 2
                        ELSE 3
          END,
          logged_on;
questions.simple: Think of a hospital queue: the most serious patients go first, not the ones whose names come first in the alphabet. Words like HIGH and LOW sort like dictionary words, so LOW would come before MEDIUM. The CASE gives each word a number, 1, 2 or 3, and the list is sorted by that number. Then the oldest complaint goes first inside each group.
questions.remember: CASE in ORDER BY = your own sort order.
questions.why: ORDER BY on a VARCHAR2 column sorts by character value, so 'LOW' comes before 'MEDIUM'. A CASE expression in ORDER BY maps each value to a rank number, giving a business order without changing the table. The second sort key, logged_on, breaks ties inside each rank.
questions.tip: When a status column has a business order, I sort with a CASE expression or join to a small lookup table that stores the rank.

steps.say: Step one. Select the complaint id, city and priority from the complaints table.
Step two. The CASE turns HIGH into one, MEDIUM into two, and everything else into three.
steps.find: ORDER  BY CASE priority WHEN 'HIGH'   THEN 1

steps.say: Finally, inside each priority, the oldest complaint comes first by logged on date.

questions.title: Black Friday deals over 40 percent
questions.scenario: An Indian shopping app is running its Black Friday sale. Marketing wants a banner of products with a discount of 40 percent or more, biggest discount first. All prices are sample data.
questions.schema:
SALE_ITEMS(item_id    VARCHAR2(3),
           product    VARCHAR2(20),
           mrp        NUMBER,   -- list price in rupees
           sale_price NUMBER)   -- Black Friday price
questions.output_note: Smartwatch is exactly 40 percent, so >= keeps it. The alias discount_pct cannot be used in WHERE, so the formula is repeated.
questions.task: Show product and discount_pct, the discount percent rounded to 1 decimal, for items with at least 40 percent off. Biggest discount first.
questions.hint: WHERE runs before SELECT, so repeat the formula there instead of using the alias.
questions.solution:
SELECT product,
       ROUND((mrp - sale_price) * 100 / mrp, 1) AS discount_pct
FROM   sale_items
WHERE  (mrp - sale_price) * 100 / mrp >= 40
ORDER  BY discount_pct DESC;
questions.simple: Imagine a price tag that says 100 rupees, and you pay 60. You saved 40 out of 100, which is 40 percent. The query does that sum for every product, keeps only the ones with 40 percent or more off, and puts the biggest savings at the top.
questions.remember: WHERE cannot see SELECT aliases; ORDER BY can.
questions.why: Oracle evaluates WHERE before the SELECT list, so a column alias like discount_pct does not exist yet in WHERE and raises ORA-00904. ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so it can use the alias. Filtering on the unrounded value avoids rounding pushing a 39.96 percent item over the line.
questions.tip: I repeat the expression in WHERE or wrap the query in an inline view, because aliases are only visible in ORDER BY.

steps.say: Step one. Work out the discount: money saved, times one hundred, divided by the price tag, rounded to one decimal.
Step two. Keep only items with forty percent or more off. We repeat the formula, because WHERE cannot see the alias.
Finally, sort so the biggest discount comes first. Wireless earbuds win at sixty percent.

trend.hook: Black Friday deals are live in India. Can you find the 40 percent discounts with SQL?

questions.title: Who let the subscription lapse?
questions.scenario: A video streaming app sells monthly plans. If a user renews the day after a plan ends, there is no break. The growth team wants every lapse: the plan end, the next start and the days without a plan.
questions.schema:
SUBSCRIPTIONS(user_id    VARCHAR2(3),
              plan_start DATE,
              plan_end   DATE)   -- last day of access
questions.output_note: U1 renewed on 01-09 straight after 31-08, so that is not a lapse. U3 has no next plan, LEAD returns NULL and the row is dropped.
questions.task: For each lapse, return user_id, plan_end, next_start and gap_days (full days with no plan). Order by user_id, plan_end.
questions.hint: LEAD(plan_start) gives the start of the user's next plan on the same row.
questions.solution:
SELECT user_id, plan_end, next_start,
       next_start - plan_end - 1 AS gap_days
FROM  (SELECT user_id, plan_end,
              LEAD(plan_start) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id
                                     ORDER BY plan_start) AS next_start
       FROM   subscriptions)
WHERE  next_start - plan_end > 1
ORDER  BY user_id, plan_end;
questions.simple: Think of a library card that runs out. If you renew it the very next morning, you never lost access. LEAD lets each plan peek at the start date of the same person's next plan. If the next plan starts more than one day after the old one ended, there were days with no plan, and we count them.
questions.remember: LEAD = peek at the next row in my group.
questions.why: LEAD(plan_start) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY plan_start) puts the next plan start on the current row. Subtracting two DATEs gives days, so a renewal the next day gives 1 and only a difference above 1 is a lapse. The last plan per user has a NULL next_start, and NULL > 1 is unknown, so it is filtered out.
questions.tip: For churn or lapse questions I compare each period to the next one with LEAD inside an inline view, then filter outside it.

steps.say: Step one. LEAD grabs the start date of the same user's next plan and puts it on this row.
Step two. A renewal the very next day is a difference of one. Bigger than one means a lapse.
Finally, count the empty days. User U1 waited five days, and U2 waited fifteen.

questions.title: Rank IPOs by listing gain
questions.scenario: A broking firm's IPO desk ranks this month's listings by listing-day gain for a client report. One IPO has not listed yet, so its listing price is NULL. All names and prices are sample data.
questions.schema:
IPO_LISTINGS(ipo_name      VARCHAR2(20),
             issue_price   NUMBER,
             listing_price NUMBER)   -- NULL = not listed yet
questions.output_note: Without NULLS LAST, Oracle sorts NULLs first in DESC order and UrbanCart Tech would be ranked 1. Two IPOs tie at 25 percent, so RANK skips 3.
questions.task: Show ipo_name, gain_pct (listing gain percent, 1 decimal) and gain_rank, best gain first. The unlisted IPO must be ranked last.
questions.hint: In a DESC sort Oracle puts NULLs first unless you say otherwise.
questions.solution:
SELECT ipo_name,
       ROUND((listing_price - issue_price) * 100 / issue_price, 1) AS gain_pct,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY (listing_price - issue_price) / issue_price
                    DESC NULLS LAST) AS gain_rank
FROM   ipo_listings
ORDER  BY gain_rank, ipo_name;
questions.simple: Imagine a race where one runner has not finished yet. You would not give that runner the gold medal just because there is no time on the board. Oracle treats an empty value as bigger than everything when sorting high to low, so it would come first. NULLS LAST sends the unfinished runner to the end of the list.
questions.remember: DESC puts NULLs on top; add NULLS LAST.
questions.why: Oracle treats NULL as higher than any value when sorting, so ORDER BY ... DESC returns NULLs first by default. Any arithmetic with a NULL listing price gives NULL, so the unlisted IPO would grab rank 1. DESC NULLS LAST fixes this, and RANK gives tied gains the same rank and skips the next number.
questions.tip: Whenever I sort descending on a nullable column, I write NULLS LAST explicitly, because the default puts NULLs at the top.

steps.say: Step one. Work out the listing gain: listing price minus issue price, as a percent of the issue price.
Step two. Rank by gain, highest first. NULLS LAST pushes the unlisted IPO to the bottom.
Finally, Kaveri and Sahyadri tie at twenty five percent, so both are rank two and rank three is skipped.

trend.hook: New IPOs are listing every week. Rank their listing gains with one SQL query.

questions.concept: Odd and even readings per day
questions.title: Odd versus even temperature readings
questions.scenario: A cold-chain warehouse in Bhiwandi logs cold-room temperatures a few times a day, but rows arrive out of order. The auditor wants, per day, the total of the 1st, 3rd, 5th reading versus the 2nd, 4th reading by time.
questions.schema:
COLD_ROOM_READINGS(reading_time DATE,          -- date and time
                   temp_c       NUMBER(4,1))
questions.output_note: On 24-11 the readings in time order are 2, 4, 3.5, 3: odd positions give 2 + 3.5 = 5.5, even positions give 4 + 3 = 7.
questions.task: For each day return day, odd_sum (readings in odd positions by time) and even_sum (even positions). Order by day.
questions.hint: Number the readings per day with ROW_NUMBER, then split with MOD(rn, 2).
questions.solution:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT TRUNC(reading_time) AS day, temp_c,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY TRUNC(reading_time)
                            ORDER BY reading_time) AS rn
  FROM   cold_room_readings
)
SELECT day,
       SUM(CASE WHEN MOD(rn, 2) = 1 THEN temp_c ELSE 0 END) AS odd_sum,
       SUM(CASE WHEN MOD(rn, 2) = 0 THEN temp_c ELSE 0 END) AS even_sum
FROM   r
GROUP  BY day
ORDER  BY day;
questions.simple: Think of kids lining up by arrival time and counting off one, two, one, two. ROW_NUMBER gives each reading its place in the day's line, by clock time, not by the order rows were saved. MOD tells us if the number is odd or even. Then we add up the odd ones and the even ones separately.
questions.remember: ROW_NUMBER to count off, MOD 2 to split odd and even.
questions.why: ROW_NUMBER partitioned by TRUNC(reading_time) and ordered by the timestamp gives the true position within each day, independent of insert order. MOD(rn, 2) classifies positions, and conditional SUM with CASE pivots them into two columns in one pass. TRUNC removes the time part so all readings of a day share one group.
questions.tip: When a question says nth event per day, I number rows with ROW_NUMBER partitioned by TRUNC of the timestamp and then aggregate with CASE.

steps.say: Step one. Number each day's readings by clock time, so the out of order rows line up correctly.
Step two. MOD of the number by two tells odd from even. Add odd positions into one total.
steps.find: SUM(CASE WHEN MOD(rn, 2) = 1 THEN temp_c ELSE 0 END) AS odd_sum

steps.say: Step three. Add the even positions into a second total.
steps.find: SUM(CASE WHEN MOD(rn, 2) = 0 THEN temp_c ELSE 0 END) AS even_sum

steps.say: Finally, group by day. On the twenty fourth, odd readings total five point five and even readings total seven.

questions.title: Add deliveries to store stock
questions.scenario: A supermarket chain loads truck deliveries into store stock. If the store already stocks the item, the quantity is added; if not, a new stock row is created. One new item arrives in two deliveries.
questions.schema:
STOCK(store_id VARCHAR2(3), sku VARCHAR2(10), qty NUMBER)
DELIVERIES(delivery_id NUMBER, store_id VARCHAR2(3),
           sku VARCHAR2(10), qty NUMBER)
questions.output_note: STOCK after the block. Delivery 3 updates 0 rows, so ATTA10KG is inserted with 15; delivery 4 then finds that row and adds 5.
questions.task: Run the block. What does the STOCK table contain afterwards?
questions.hint: SQL%ROWCOUNT tells you how many rows the last UPDATE changed.
questions.simple: Think of a shopkeeper with a notebook page for each item. When a delivery comes, he looks for that item's page and adds the new count. If there is no page yet, he starts a new page. The block tries to add to the page first, and SQL%ROWCOUNT tells it whether a page was found. If not, it writes a new row.
questions.remember: UPDATE first; SQL%ROWCOUNT = 0 means insert.
questions.why: SQL%ROWCOUNT is an implicit cursor attribute holding the number of rows affected by the most recent DML statement. An UPDATE that matches nothing is not an error, it just sets SQL%ROWCOUNT to 0, so the code can fall back to INSERT. Because the loop processes deliveries in order, the row inserted for delivery 3 is visible to the UPDATE for delivery 4 in the same transaction.
questions.tip: For row-by-row upserts I update first and check SQL%ROWCOUNT, but for set-based loads I'd use a single MERGE.

steps.say: Step one. Go through deliveries in order, and try to add the quantity to the existing stock row.
Step two. If the update touched zero rows, the store does not stock that item yet, so insert a new row.
Finally, atta was inserted with fifteen, then the next delivery updated it to twenty.

questions.title: Game purchases with custom errors
questions.scenario: A mobile game lets players buy items with coins. A purchase procedure raises a custom error when coins are short. The batch logs OK or the error for each purchase and keeps going.
questions.schema:
WALLETS(player_id VARCHAR2(3), coins NUMBER)
PURCHASES(purchase_id NUMBER, player_id VARCHAR2(3),
          item_cost NUMBER)
PURCHASE_LOG(player_id VARCHAR2(3), msg VARCHAR2(60))
questions.output_note: PURCHASE_LOG after the block; WALLETS ends as P1 = 200, P2 = 120. P1 had only 200 left for purchase 3, and P9 has no wallet, so SELECT INTO raises NO_DATA_FOUND (SQLCODE 100).
questions.task: Run the block. What rows end up in PURCHASE_LOG?
questions.hint: RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR sets SQLCODE to your number and SQLERRM to ORA-<number>: <your message>.
questions.simple: Think of a toy shop where you pay with tokens from a piggy bank. If you do not have enough tokens, the shopkeeper says 'Not enough coins' and gives you a slip with error number 20001. If you have no piggy bank at all, you get a different slip. The block writes down every slip in a notebook and serves the next child.
questions.remember: RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR = your own error number and message.
questions.why: RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR raises a user-defined exception with a code from -20000 to -20999, and SQLERRM returns it as ORA-20001: message. The inner BEGIN-EXCEPTION block catches it per purchase, so the loop continues. Purchase 3 fails because purchase 1 already reduced P1 to 200 coins, and the unknown player triggers NO_DATA_FOUND, whose SQLCODE is +100.
questions.tip: I use RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR with documented -20xxx codes for business rules, and log SQLCODE and SQLERRM in batch jobs so one bad row does not stop the run.

steps.say: Step one. Read the player's coins. If there are not enough, raise our own error, number twenty thousand and one.
steps.find: SELECT coins INTO v_coins FROM wallets WHERE player_id = p_player;

steps.say: Step two. P1 buys for three hundred, coins drop to two hundred, and we log OK.
Step three. Any error is caught here and logged with its code and message, so the loop keeps going.
steps.to: INSERT INTO purchase_log VALUES (p.player_id, SQLCODE || ' ' || SQLERRM);

steps.say: Finally, P9 has no wallet, so we log one hundred, no data found.

questions.title: Weighted FD rate per branch
questions.scenario: A bank’s ALM team needs the average fixed deposit rate per branch and for the whole bank. A small FD at a low rate should not pull the average down as much as a big FD.
questions.schema:
FD_ACCOUNTS(fd_id  VARCHAR2(3),
            branch VARCHAR2(15),
            amount NUMBER,        -- principal in rupees
            rate   NUMBER(4,2))   -- annual rate %
questions.output_note: A plain AVG(rate) would give 6.83 for Jaipur and 6.77 overall, which understates the cost of deposits.
questions.task: Show branch_name, total_amount and wavg_rate (amount-weighted rate, 2 decimals) per branch plus a grand total row labelled ALL BRANCHES, which comes last.
questions.hint: Weighted average = SUM(amount * rate) / SUM(amount); ROLLUP adds the total row.
questions.solution:
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(branch) = 1 THEN 'ALL BRANCHES'
            ELSE branch END                       AS branch_name,
       SUM(amount)                                AS total_amount,
       ROUND(SUM(amount * rate) / SUM(amount), 2) AS wavg_rate
FROM   fd_accounts
GROUP  BY ROLLUP (branch)
ORDER  BY GROUPING(branch), branch;
questions.simple: Imagine a class where one big group of 10 kids scored 90 and one kid scored 50. The fair class average is close to 90, not 70, because more kids scored 90. Here every rupee is like one kid: big deposits count more. ROLLUP then adds one extra line with the total for the whole bank.
questions.remember: Weighted average = SUM(value x weight) / SUM(weight).
questions.why: AVG(rate) gives every FD equal weight, while the bank pays interest per rupee, so SUM(amount * rate) / SUM(amount) is the correct cost of funds. GROUP BY ROLLUP(branch) adds a super-aggregate row where branch is NULL, and GROUPING(branch) = 1 identifies it reliably even if real data had NULL branches. Ordering by GROUPING(branch) puts the total last.
questions.tip: For rates, prices or yields across different sizes I always use a weighted average, and I label ROLLUP total rows with GROUPING, not NVL.

steps.say: Step one. Multiply each amount by its rate, add them up, and divide by the total amount. That is the weighted rate.
Step two. ROLLUP gives one row per branch, plus one extra row for the whole bank.
Step three. GROUPING is one only on that extra row, so we label it ALL BRANCHES.
steps.find: SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(branch) = 1 THEN 'ALL BRANCHES'

steps.say: Finally, Jaipur comes out at seven point one two, higher than a plain average, because the big deposit earns the most.

questions.title: Find flats nobody has booked
questions.scenario: A builder in Pune, Hyderabad and Noida tracks flats in one table and bookings in another. The sales head wants the list of flats that are still unsold.
questions.schema:
FLATS(flat_id    VARCHAR2(5),
      project    VARCHAR2(15),
      city       VARCHAR2(15),
      price_lakh NUMBER)        -- price in lakh rupees
BOOKINGS(booking_id NUMBER,
         flat_id    VARCHAR2(5),  -- booked flat
         booked_on  DATE)
questions.task: Show flat_id, project and price_lakh of every flat that has no booking, ordered by flat_id.
questions.hint: Keep a flat only if NOT EXISTS finds no matching booking row.
questions.solution:
SELECT f.flat_id, f.project, f.price_lakh
FROM   flats f
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                   FROM   bookings b
                   WHERE  b.flat_id = f.flat_id)
ORDER  BY f.flat_id;
questions.simple: Think of a school trip list and a list of kids who paid. To find who has not paid, you take each kid and look for their name on the paid list. If it is not there, they go on the reminder list. NOT EXISTS does the same for each flat.
questions.remember: NOT EXISTS = keep me if nobody matches me.
questions.why: NOT EXISTS runs the correlated subquery for each outer row and keeps the row when the subquery returns nothing. It is NULL-safe, unlike NOT IN, which returns no rows if the subquery ever yields a NULL flat_id. The optimizer usually turns it into an anti-join.
questions.tip: For 'rows with no match' I prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN because a single NULL makes NOT IN return nothing.

steps.say: Step one. Go through every flat in the flats table.
Step two. For each flat, look for a booking with the same flat id.
Finally, flats with no booking stay. A102 and B202 are still unsold.

questions.title: Busiest clinic days of the week
questions.scenario: A clinic in Bengaluru wants to know which weekdays get the most appointments, so it can add a doctor on busy days.
questions.schema:
APPOINTMENTS(appt_id   NUMBER,
             doctor    VARCHAR2(15),
             appt_date DATE)          -- day of the visit
questions.output_note: 23-11 and 30-11 are both Mondays, so they add up. Day names assume English NLS settings.
questions.task: Show day_name (MON, TUE, ...) and appts, the number of appointments on that weekday, busiest first; break ties by day_name.
questions.hint: TO_CHAR(appt_date, 'DY') turns a date into its short day name; group by that.
questions.solution:
SELECT TO_CHAR(appt_date, 'DY') AS day_name,
       COUNT(*)                 AS appts
FROM   appointments
GROUP  BY TO_CHAR(appt_date, 'DY')
ORDER  BY appts DESC, day_name;
questions.simple: Imagine a calendar where you only look at the day names, not the dates. Every Monday goes into the Monday box, every Saturday into the Saturday box. Then you count the slips in each box. TO_CHAR gives the day name and GROUP BY makes the boxes.
questions.remember: TO_CHAR(date, 'DY') = which day of the week?
questions.why: TO_CHAR(appt_date, 'DY') returns the abbreviated weekday, so different dates that share a weekday fall into one group. The GROUP BY must repeat the expression because the column alias is not visible there in Oracle. The output language depends on NLS_DATE_LANGUAGE, which can be passed as a third argument.
questions.tip: When I group by weekday I either repeat the TO_CHAR expression in GROUP BY or wrap it in a subquery, since Oracle does not allow the alias there.

steps.say: Step one. Turn each date into its day name, like MON or SAT.
Step two. Group by that day name and count the visits in each group.
Finally, sort busiest first. Monday and Saturday tie with three visits each.

questions.concept: LEFT JOIN with NVL on SUM
questions.title: Purse left after the auction
questions.scenario: It is IPL auction season. Each team starts with a purse in crore rupees and buys players. The analyst wants every team's spend, even a team that bought nobody.
questions.schema:
TEAMS(team_code VARCHAR2(3),
      team_name VARCHAR2(20),
      purse_cr  NUMBER(6,2))    -- starting purse, crore
BIDS(player    VARCHAR2(20),
     team_code VARCHAR2(3),     -- buying team
     price_cr  NUMBER(6,2))     -- winning bid, crore
questions.output_note: Teams, players and amounts are made-up sample data. COUNT(*) would wrongly show 1 player for Pune Panthers.
questions.task: Show team_name, players_bought and purse_left (purse minus total bids) for every team, including teams with no buys, most money left first.
questions.hint: LEFT JOIN keeps Pune; count a BIDS column and wrap SUM in NVL.
questions.solution:
SELECT t.team_name,
       COUNT(b.player)                      AS players_bought,
       t.purse_cr - NVL(SUM(b.price_cr), 0) AS purse_left
FROM   teams t
LEFT   JOIN bids b ON b.team_code = t.team_code
GROUP  BY t.team_name, t.purse_cr
ORDER  BY purse_left DESC;
questions.simple: Each team gets pocket money before going shopping. Some kids buy a lot, one kid buys nothing. The LEFT JOIN makes sure the kid who bought nothing is still on the list. NVL says 'nothing spent means zero spent', so we can still do the subtraction.
questions.remember: LEFT JOIN keeps everyone; NVL turns 'nothing' into zero.
questions.why: A LEFT JOIN keeps Pune Panthers with NULL bid columns, so SUM(b.price_cr) is NULL and purse minus NULL would be NULL; NVL(..., 0) fixes that. COUNT(b.player) ignores NULLs and gives 0, while COUNT(*) counts the outer-joined row and gives 1. purse_cr must be in GROUP BY because it is used outside an aggregate.
questions.tip: With an outer join I count a column from the optional table, never COUNT(*), and I wrap its SUM in NVL.

steps.say: Step one. LEFT JOIN keeps every team, even Pune who bought nobody.
steps.find: LEFT   JOIN bids b ON b.team_code = t.team_code

steps.say: Step two. Count the player column, so Pune shows zero, not one.
Step three. NVL turns Pune's empty spend into zero before we subtract.
Finally, sort by money left. Pune Panthers top the list with nine point seven five crore.

trend.hook: The IPL auction is coming! Which team still has the most money left? Let SQL find out.

questions.concept: Join to a single-day rate row
questions.title: Gold loans breaching 75% LTV
questions.scenario: Gold prices have been falling this month. A bank's gold-loan desk must flag loans whose loan-to-value crosses 75% at today's rate, so branches can ask for top-ups.
questions.schema:
GOLD_RATES(rate_date  DATE,
           rate_per_g NUMBER)     -- 22K rate, rupees per gram
GOLD_LOANS(loan_id     VARCHAR2(4),
           customer    VARCHAR2(15),
           gold_g      NUMBER,    -- pledged gold in grams
           outstanding NUMBER)    -- loan balance in rupees
questions.output_note: All rates are invented sample data, not real prices. Farah is exactly 75.00% and is not flagged; at the 24-11 rate no loan crossed 75%.
questions.task: Using the rate for 27-11-2026, show loan_id, customer, gold_value and ltv_pct (outstanding / gold value x 100, 2 decimals) for loans above 75%, highest LTV first.
questions.hint: Join each loan to the one GOLD_RATES row for 27-11-2026, then compare the ratio with 75.
questions.solution:
SELECT l.loan_id, l.customer,
       l.gold_g * r.rate_per_g AS gold_value,
       ROUND(l.outstanding * 100 / (l.gold_g * r.rate_per_g), 2) AS ltv_pct
FROM   gold_loans l
JOIN   gold_rates r ON r.rate_date = DATE '2026-11-27'
WHERE  l.outstanding * 100 / (l.gold_g * r.rate_per_g) > 75
ORDER  BY ltv_pct DESC;
questions.simple: Imagine you borrowed money and gave your gold chain as a promise. If the chain's value drops, your loan becomes too big compared to the chain. We take today's gold price, find each chain's value, and see how big the loan is compared to it. Anyone above 75 out of 100 gets a call.
questions.remember: LTV = loan divided by today's collateral value.
questions.why: The join condition only filters GOLD_RATES to one row, so every loan pairs with exactly that day's rate; if the date were missing the join would return nothing, and two rows for the date would double every loan. The WHERE clause repeats the unrounded expression because the alias ltv_pct is not visible in WHERE, and comparing unrounded values avoids a 75.004 being rounded down. The > keeps the exact 75% loan out.
questions.tip: For collateral checks I join to the rate as of a fixed date and filter on the unrounded ratio, rounding only for display.

steps.say: Step one. Pick only today's gold rate and pair it with every loan.
steps.find: JOIN   gold_rates r ON r.rate_date = DATE '2026-11-27'

steps.say: Step two. Gold value is grams times rate. LTV is the loan divided by that value, times one hundred.
Step three. Keep only loans above seventy-five percent. Farah at exactly seventy-five is safe.
Finally, Vikram and Suresh need a top-up, because falling gold pushed them over the limit.

trend.hook: Gold prices keep falling. Which gold loans just crossed the danger line? One SQL query tells you.

questions.concept: Nth row per user with ROW_NUMBER
questions.title: Each customer's third card swipe
questions.scenario: A card issuer runs an offer on every customer's third card transaction. Two swipes can share the same timestamp, so the order must still be fixed.
questions.schema:
CARD_TXNS(txn_id   NUMBER,       -- increasing id
          customer VARCHAR2(10),
          txn_time DATE,         -- swipe time
          amount   NUMBER)       -- rupees
questions.output_note: With RANK, Bilal's 106 and 107 would both be rank 2 and he would have no rank 3. Chitra has only one swipe, so she is left out.
questions.task: Show customer, txn_id, txn_time and amount of each customer's third transaction by time; if times tie, the lower txn_id comes first. Skip customers with fewer than three.
questions.hint: ROW_NUMBER per customer ordered by txn_time, txn_id, then keep rn = 3.
questions.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT customer, txn_id, txn_time, amount,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer
                            ORDER BY txn_time, txn_id) AS rn
  FROM   card_txns
)
SELECT customer, txn_id, txn_time, amount
FROM   ranked
WHERE  rn = 3
ORDER  BY customer;
questions.simple: Think of kids lining up for ice cream, and every third kid gets a free scoop. If two kids arrive at the same moment, the teacher decides by roll number. ROW_NUMBER gives each swipe a place in the line, one line per customer. Then we just pick place number three.
questions.remember: Nth per group = ROW_NUMBER with a tie-breaker, then rn = N.
questions.why: ROW_NUMBER always gives distinct numbers 1, 2, 3 within each PARTITION BY group, so exactly one row can be third; RANK and DENSE_RANK repeat numbers on ties and can skip or duplicate the third row. Adding txn_id to ORDER BY makes the numbering deterministic when timestamps tie. The filter must be in an outer query because window functions are computed after WHERE.
questions.tip: For 'Nth event per user' I use ROW_NUMBER with a unique tie-breaker in the ORDER BY, and filter in an outer query.

steps.say: Step one. Split swipes by customer, and number them in time order.
steps.to: ORDER BY txn_time, txn_id) AS rn

steps.say: Step two. When two swipes share a time, the smaller transaction id goes first.
steps.find: ORDER BY txn_time, txn_id) AS rn

steps.say: Step three. In the outer query, keep only swipe number three.
Finally, Asha gets 103 and Bilal gets 107. Chitra has only one swipe, so she is out.

questions.title: Grade all students in batches
questions.scenario: An ed-tech platform grades exam scores in batches with BULK COLLECT LIMIT. A wrongly placed EXIT once skipped the last few students, so the loop must handle a final small batch.
questions.schema:
EXAM_SCORES(roll_no NUMBER,
            student VARCHAR2(15),
            marks   NUMBER)       -- out of 100, pass at 40
RESULTS(roll_no NUMBER,
        grade   VARCHAR2(4))     -- PASS or FAIL, empty at start
questions.output_note: RESULTS after the block. Batches are 2, 2 and 1 rows; with EXIT WHEN c%NOTFOUND right after the FETCH, Esha's last batch of 1 would be skipped.
questions.task: Write a PL/SQL block that reads EXAM_SCORES 2 rows at a time with BULK COLLECT LIMIT and inserts PASS (marks >= 40) or FAIL into RESULTS with FORALL, without losing the last partial batch.
questions.hint: Exit when the fetched collection is empty, not when %NOTFOUND is true.
questions.simple: Imagine a teacher carrying answer sheets two at a time from one room to another. On the last trip there is only one sheet left. A careless teacher sees 'pile is finished' and stops before carrying it. The right rule is: stop only when your hands come back empty.
questions.remember: With LIMIT, exit when COUNT = 0, not on %NOTFOUND.
questions.why: On the fetch that returns fewer rows than LIMIT, %NOTFOUND is already TRUE even though the collection holds rows, so EXIT WHEN c%NOTFOUND right after FETCH drops the last partial batch. Checking l_rolls.COUNT = 0 exits only after an empty fetch. FORALL sends each batch of inserts to the SQL engine in one context switch.
questions.tip: In BULK COLLECT LIMIT loops I put EXIT WHEN coll.COUNT = 0 after the fetch, or EXIT WHEN c%NOTFOUND at the bottom after processing.

steps.say: Step one. Fetch the students two at a time into two collections.
steps.find: FETCH c BULK COLLECT INTO l_rolls, l_marks LIMIT 2;

steps.say: Step two. Stop only when a fetch brings back nothing. The last trip with one student still gets processed.
Step three. FORALL inserts the whole batch, with PASS at forty or more.
steps.to: VALUES (l_rolls(i), CASE WHEN l_marks(i) >= 40 THEN 'PASS' ELSE 'FAIL' END);

steps.say: Finally, all five students get a grade, including Esha in the last batch.

questions.title: Migrate plans without crashing
questions.scenario: A telecom operator moves prepaid users from old plans to new ones. One user has an unknown plan code, and the job must log it instead of failing the whole run.
questions.schema:
SUBSCRIBERS(msisdn    VARCHAR2(10),
            plan_code VARCHAR2(5),   -- old plan
            new_plan  VARCHAR2(5))   -- NULL until migrated
MIGRATION_LOG(msisdn VARCHAR2(10),
              msg    VARCHAR2(50))  -- empty at start
questions.output_note: SUBSCRIBERS after the block; MIGRATION_LOG gets one row: 9810000003, 'Unknown plan P99X'. Without the ELSE, P99X raises ORA-06592 CASE_NOT_FOUND and the whole block's changes are rolled back.
questions.task: Write a block that maps P199 to N239, P299 to N349 and P499 to N549 using a CASE statement, and logs any other plan code into MIGRATION_LOG instead of raising an error.
questions.hint: A PL/SQL CASE statement with no matching WHEN and no ELSE raises CASE_NOT_FOUND.
questions.simple: Think of a post office sorting letters into boxes by city. If a letter has a city with no box, a strict sorter throws up his hands and stops the whole sorting. A smart sorter puts it in a 'problem' tray and keeps going. The ELSE branch is that problem tray.
questions.remember: CASE statement without ELSE = crash on the unexpected.
questions.why: A CASE expression in SQL returns NULL when nothing matches, but a PL/SQL CASE statement raises ORA-06592 CASE_NOT_FOUND instead. If that exception is unhandled, the anonymous block fails and Oracle rolls back all its uncommitted work, including earlier successful updates. An ELSE branch routes unknown codes to a log and lets the loop finish.
questions.tip: I always give a PL/SQL CASE statement an ELSE, even if it only logs or raises a clear custom error, because CASE_NOT_FOUND is easy to miss in testing.

steps.say: Step one. Loop through every subscriber and look at the old plan code.
steps.find: FOR s IN (SELECT msisdn, plan_code FROM subscribers) LOOP

steps.say: Step two. Each known code gets its new plan with a simple update.
steps.to: UPDATE subscribers SET new_plan = 'N549' WHERE msisdn = s.msisdn;

steps.say: Step three. Any other code goes to the log. Without this ELSE, the block crashes with case not found.
Finally, three users move to new plans and P99X is logged for a human to check.

questions.title: Catch overlapping crew duties
questions.scenario: An airline's rostering team must make sure no crew member is on two flights at once. Back-to-back duties that just touch are allowed.
questions.schema:
CREW_DUTIES(duty_id    VARCHAR2(3),
            crew_id    VARCHAR2(3),
            flight     VARCHAR2(6),
            duty_start DATE,         -- sign-on time
            duty_end   DATE)         -- sign-off time
questions.output_note: D2 and D3 only touch at 12:00, so they are not an overlap. D5 sits fully inside D4 and is still caught.
questions.task: List crew_id, duty_a, duty_b and overlap_min (minutes of overlap) for every pair of duties of the same crew member that overlap, each pair once.
questions.hint: Two ranges overlap when each one starts before the other ends.
questions.solution:
SELECT a.crew_id, a.duty_id AS duty_a, b.duty_id AS duty_b,
       ROUND((LEAST(a.duty_end, b.duty_end)
            - GREATEST(a.duty_start, b.duty_start)) * 24 * 60) AS overlap_min
FROM   crew_duties a
JOIN   crew_duties b
  ON   b.crew_id    = a.crew_id
 AND   b.duty_id    > a.duty_id
 AND   b.duty_start < a.duty_end
 AND   a.duty_start < b.duty_end
ORDER  BY a.crew_id, a.duty_id;
questions.simple: Imagine two cricket practice slots booked for the same kid. If one slot starts before the other finishes, and the other starts before the first finishes, the kid would need to be in two places. We compare every pair of slots for the same kid. If one ends exactly when the next begins, that is fine.
questions.remember: Overlap: A starts before B ends AND B starts before A ends.
questions.why: The self-join pairs each duty with the other duties of the same crew, and b.duty_id > a.duty_id keeps each pair once and skips self-pairs. The two strict < conditions cover partial and full containment while treating touching ranges as not overlapping. Subtracting Oracle DATEs gives days, so * 24 * 60 converts the overlap from LEAST(end) - GREATEST(start) into minutes.
questions.tip: For any booking or roster clash I use the two-condition overlap test, start_a < end_b AND start_b < end_a, instead of listing every case.

steps.say: Step one. Join the duties table to itself, for the same crew member, each pair only once.
Step two. They overlap if each duty starts before the other one ends.
Step three. Overlap is the earlier end minus the later start, turned into minutes.
Finally, D1 and D2 clash by thirty minutes, and D5 sits inside D4 for sixty.

lessons.why: LAST_VALUE silently returns the current row's value unless you widen the window, a common bug in month-end and closing-rate reports.
lessons.explain: When an analytic function has ORDER BY but no frame, Oracle uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. For SUM that gives a running total, but for LAST_VALUE it means the last row seen so far is the current row, so you get the row's own value back. To get the true last value of the partition, state ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or use FIRST_VALUE with ORDER BY ... DESC. Adding IGNORE NULLS turns it into a carry-forward tool.
lessons.example:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-02' d, 83.10 rate FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-03', 83.25 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT DATE '2026-11-04', 83.18 FROM dual
)
SELECT d, rate,
       LAST_VALUE(rate) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS default_frame,
       LAST_VALUE(rate) OVER (ORDER BY d
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS closing_rate
FROM r;
-- default_frame: 83.10, 83.25, 83.18   closing_rate: 83.18, 83.18, 83.18
lessons.gotcha: LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (ORDER BY d) looks right in a quick test but just echoes x on every row.
lessons.line: For a closing value per period I use LAST_VALUE with an explicit UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame, or FIRST_VALUE ordered descending, because the default frame stops at the current row.
lessons.simple: LAST_VALUE sounds like 'give me the last one', but by default it only looks from the top down to the current row, so the last one it sees is itself. To see the real last row, tell it to look all the way to the end.
lessons.remember: Tell LAST_VALUE to look to the end: UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

lessons.why: Top-N queries written with ROWNUM in the same SELECT as ORDER BY return the wrong rows, a classic interview trap and a real reporting bug.
lessons.simple: Imagine a teacher who hands out medals to the first 2 children who walk in, and only after that lines them up by height. The medal winners were never the tallest, just the first through the door. ROWNUM is that door number: Oracle gives it out before ORDER BY sorts. So sort first in an inner query, then hand out the numbers.
lessons.remember: ROWNUM is given before sorting; sort inside, filter outside.
lessons.explain: ROWNUM is assigned to each row as it passes the WHERE clause, before ORDER BY runs, so WHERE ROWNUM <= 2 ... ORDER BY bal DESC picks any two rows and then sorts just those. The fix is to sort in an inline view and apply ROWNUM outside it, or in 12c and later use ORDER BY ... FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY (or ROW_NUMBER() OVER for top-N per group). WHERE ROWNUM > 1 never returns anything, because the first row fails, so the next row becomes ROWNUM 1 again. FETCH FIRST n ROWS WITH TIES also keeps rows tied with the last one.
lessons.gotcha: SELECT ... WHERE ROWNUM <= 5 ORDER BY amount DESC returns five random rows sorted, not the top five.
lessons.line: Because ROWNUM is assigned before ORDER BY, I either sort in an inline view and filter ROWNUM outside, or simply use FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY.

lessons.why: Picking the wrong ranking function on tied values is one of the most common interview traps in top-N and Nth-highest questions.
lessons.simple: Think of a race where two runners cross the line together. ROW_NUMBER is the strict referee who still gives them 1 and 2. RANK gives both of them 1 and the next runner 3, skipping 2. DENSE_RANK gives both of them 1 and the next runner 2, without skipping. All three just put numbers on rows in the order you ask for.
lessons.remember: ROW_NUMBER unique, RANK skips, DENSE_RANK never skips.
lessons.explain: All three are analytic functions that need OVER (ORDER BY ...) and can restart per group with PARTITION BY. ROW_NUMBER always gives 1, 2, 3 even on ties, so which tied row gets the lower number is not deterministic unless you add a tie-breaker column. RANK gives tied rows the same number and then jumps (1, 1, 3), while DENSE_RANK gives the same number and continues (1, 1, 2). Use ROW_NUMBER for de-duplication or exactly-N rows, RANK for 'positions' like a competition, and DENSE_RANK for 'Nth highest distinct value'.
lessons.example:
WITH b AS (
  SELECT 'Arun' cust, 90000 bal FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Bina', 90000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Chetan', 70000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Divya', 50000 FROM dual
)
SELECT cust, bal,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC, cust) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC)       AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY bal DESC)       AS drnk
FROM   b;
-- Arun 90000 1 1 1 | Bina 90000 2 1 1 | Chetan 70000 3 3 2 | Divya 50000 4 4 3
lessons.gotcha: Using ROW_NUMBER = 1 to find 'the top customer' silently drops a customer who is tied for first place.
lessons.line: I pick ROW_NUMBER when I need exactly one row per group, RANK when ties should share a position with gaps, and DENSE_RANK for Nth-highest distinct values.

lessons.why: Interviewers often ask for a total next to each detail row, and choosing GROUP BY instead of an analytic function loses the detail rows.
lessons.simple: Think of a class photo and a class report card. GROUP BY is the report card: one line per class with the total, and the children's names disappear. OVER (PARTITION BY) is the class photo with a sticker on each child showing the class total: every child is still there. Use GROUP BY for summaries and OVER when you need the details plus the total.
lessons.remember: GROUP BY squashes rows; OVER keeps every row.
lessons.explain: GROUP BY collapses all rows with the same key into one result row, so only grouped columns and aggregates can be selected. An analytic function such as SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY branch) computes the same aggregate but returns it on every input row, without reducing the row count. Analytic functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING but before the final ORDER BY, so they cannot be used in WHERE; wrap them in an inline view to filter. You can even combine both, for example SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () to get a grand total next to grouped rows.
lessons.example:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT 'Pune' branch, 'A1' acct, 5000 amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Pune', 'A2', 3000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Nagpur', 'A3', 7000 FROM dual
)
SELECT branch, acct, amt,
       SUM(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY branch) AS branch_total,
       ROUND(100 * amt / SUM(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY branch), 1) AS pct
FROM   t
ORDER  BY branch, acct;
-- Nagpur A3 7000 7000 100 | Pune A1 5000 8000 62.5 | Pune A2 3000 8000 37.5
lessons.gotcha: Putting an analytic function in the WHERE clause raises ORA-30483; filter on it in an outer query instead.
lessons.line: I use GROUP BY when I want one row per group, and SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) when I need the group total alongside every detail row.

lessons.why: Interviewers often ask when to use EXISTS or IN, and the NOT IN version silently returns nothing when the list has a NULL.
lessons.simple: Think of a teacher asking 'is there at least one homework copy from Ravi in the pile?'. EXISTS stops looking as soon as it finds one copy, it just answers yes or no. IN first makes a list of names from the pile and checks if Ravi is on it. For finding matches both give the same answer. For 'not in the pile', a blank name on the list confuses NOT IN, but NOT EXISTS still works.
lessons.remember: EXISTS asks 'any match?'; NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe.
lessons.explain: EXISTS (correlated subquery) returns TRUE as soon as one matching row is found, and the select list inside it is ignored, so SELECT 1 is common. IN compares a value with the set returned by the subquery; for positive checks Oracle usually rewrites both into the same semi-join, so performance is often identical. The difference shows with negation: if the subquery returns any NULL, x NOT IN (...) is never TRUE and the query returns no rows, whereas NOT EXISTS is evaluated row by row and is unaffected. Oracle turns NOT EXISTS (and NOT IN on NOT NULL columns) into an anti-join.
lessons.example:
WITH acct AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A2' FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A3' FROM dual
), upi_txn AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no, 500 amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT NULL, 900 FROM dual
)
SELECT a.acct_no,
       CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM upi_txn u WHERE u.acct_no = a.acct_no)
            THEN 'Uses UPI' ELSE 'No UPI' END AS upi_status
FROM   acct a
ORDER  BY a.acct_no;
-- A1 Uses UPI | A2 No UPI | A3 No UPI
-- But WHERE acct_no NOT IN (SELECT acct_no FROM upi_txn) returns no rows because of the NULL.
lessons.gotcha: NOT IN against a subquery that can return NULL gives an empty result, so use NOT EXISTS or add WHERE col IS NOT NULL inside.
lessons.line: For positive checks IN and EXISTS usually get the same semi-join plan, but for exclusions I write NOT EXISTS because NOT IN breaks when the subquery returns a NULL.

lessons.why: Interviewers like asking the difference between NVL and COALESCE, and getting it right shows you understand NULL handling and performance.
lessons.simple: Think of a shopping bill where some prices are blank. NVL says 'if the box is empty, write this instead'. NVL2 asks 'is the box filled?' and writes one word for yes and another for no. COALESCE looks along a row of boxes and takes the first one that is filled. All three help you put something sensible where a blank would be.
lessons.remember: NVL = one backup, COALESCE = first filled box.
lessons.explain: NVL(a, b) returns b when a is NULL and always evaluates both arguments, converting b to the data type of a. NVL2(a, b, c) returns b when a is NOT NULL and c when it is NULL, which is handy for flags. COALESCE(a, b, c, ...) is ANSI standard, accepts any number of arguments, returns the first non-NULL one and stops evaluating as soon as it finds it (short-circuit). COALESCE requires all arguments to be of the same data type family, so COALESCE(number_col, 'NA') raises ORA-00932 where NVL would try an implicit conversion.
lessons.example:
WITH acct AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no, 5000 od_limit, CAST(NULL AS NUMBER) temp_limit FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A2', NULL, 20000 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A3', NULL, NULL FROM dual
)
SELECT acct_no,
       NVL(od_limit, 0)                   AS od_or_zero,
       NVL2(od_limit, 'Has OD', 'No OD')  AS od_flag,
       COALESCE(temp_limit, od_limit, 0)  AS effective_limit
FROM   acct
ORDER  BY acct_no;
-- A1 5000 Has OD 5000 | A2 0 No OD 20000 | A3 0 No OD 0
lessons.gotcha: NVL always evaluates its second argument, so NVL(col, slow_function()) calls the function for every row, while COALESCE calls it only when col is NULL.
lessons.line: I prefer COALESCE because it is ANSI, takes many arguments and short-circuits, and I use NVL2 when I need a different value for filled and empty cases.

lessons.why: Banks run the same query millions of times, and interviewers ask about bind variables to see if you can avoid a common cause of slow, CPU-hungry databases.
lessons.simple: Think of a shopping bill printed from a template where only the name and amount change. If the shop designed a brand-new bill layout for every customer, it would be very slow. A literal like acct_no = 'A1' makes Oracle plan a new query each time. A bind variable like acct_no = :acct lets Oracle reuse the same plan and just fill in the blank.
lessons.remember: Same query, new value? Use a :bind, reuse the plan.
lessons.explain: Before running a SQL statement Oracle parses it and builds an execution plan, and a hard parse (syntax check, optimisation, plan creation) is expensive and takes shared pool latches. If the SQL text differs only by a literal value, each version is a new statement and needs its own hard parse, filling the shared pool with near-duplicates. With a bind variable the text stays the same, so later executions are soft parses that reuse the cached cursor; static SQL in PL/SQL binds variables automatically, and dynamic SQL should use EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ... USING. Bind variables also prevent SQL injection, because the value is never part of the SQL text.
lessons.example:
VARIABLE acct VARCHAR2(10)
EXEC :acct := 'A2'

WITH account AS (
  SELECT 'A1' acct_no, 52000 balance FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A2', 18500 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'A3', 730000 FROM dual
)
SELECT acct_no, balance
FROM   account
WHERE  acct_no = :acct;
-- A2 18500 ; change :acct and rerun, the same cursor is reused
lessons.gotcha: Concatenating values into dynamic SQL ('... WHERE acct_no = ''' || p_acct || '''') gives a new hard parse per value and opens a SQL injection hole, so use USING binds instead.
lessons.line: I use bind variables so repeated statements are soft-parsed and share one cursor, which saves CPU and protects against SQL injection.

lessons.concept: When Oracle can use a B-tree index
lessons.why: Bank tables hold crores of rows, and interviewers check whether you know why a query on an indexed column can still scan the whole table.
lessons.simple: Think of the index at the back of a textbook: words are listed A to Z with page numbers, so you jump straight to the page. If you ask 'find words that end in -tion', the A-to-Z list cannot help and you must read every page. An Oracle index works the same way on the column's real stored values. If you change the column first (wrap it in a function, or compare text to a number), Oracle cannot use the list and reads the whole table.
lessons.remember: Leave the indexed column bare; change the value instead.
lessons.explain: A B-tree index stores column values in sorted order with ROWIDs, so Oracle can do an index range scan when the predicate compares the bare column with =, <, >, BETWEEN or a LIKE with a fixed prefix. Wrapping the column in a function such as TRUNC(txn_date) or UPPER(name), a leading wildcard LIKE '%1001', or an implicit conversion (acct_no VARCHAR2 compared with the number 1001 becomes TO_NUMBER(acct_no) = 1001) hides the stored values, so the optimizer cannot use a normal index. The fix is to rewrite the predicate on the value side (txn_date >= :d AND txn_date < :d + 1, acct_no = '1001') or create a function-based index on the exact expression. Even a usable index may be skipped if the query returns a large share of rows, because a full scan with multiblock reads is then cheaper.
lessons.example:
WITH txn AS (
  SELECT '1001' acct_no, TO_DATE('31-03-2026 10:15','DD-MM-YYYY HH24:MI') txn_date, 5000 amount FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT '1001', TO_DATE('31-03-2026 18:40','DD-MM-YYYY HH24:MI'), 1200 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT '1002', TO_DATE('01-04-2026 09:05','DD-MM-YYYY HH24:MI'), 800 FROM dual
)
SELECT acct_no, txn_date, amount
FROM   txn
WHERE  acct_no  = '1001'                  -- not acct_no = 1001
AND    txn_date >= DATE '2026-03-31'       -- not TRUNC(txn_date) = ...
AND    txn_date <  DATE '2026-04-01';
-- returns the two rows of 31-03-2026 for account 1001
lessons.gotcha: Comparing a VARCHAR2 column to a number makes Oracle apply TO_NUMBER to every row's column, which silently disables the index and can even raise ORA-01722 on non-numeric values.
lessons.line: I keep indexed columns bare in WHERE clauses, match data types to avoid implicit conversion, and use function-based indexes only when the expression cannot be moved to the value side.

lessons.why: Interviewers ask which column goes first in a multi-column index, and the answer decides whether your query uses it.
lessons.simple: Think of a phone book sorted by surname, then first name. Finding all 'Sharma' is fast, and 'Sharma, Ritu' is even faster. But finding every 'Ritu' means reading the whole book. A composite index is the same: it helps when you search by its first column.
lessons.remember: Leading column first: the index is sorted by it.
lessons.explain: A composite B-tree index on (acct_no, txn_date) is sorted by acct_no, then txn_date inside each acct_no. Queries filtering on acct_no, or acct_no plus a txn_date range, can do a fast range scan. A filter on txn_date alone cannot seek directly; Oracle may use an index skip scan only if acct_no has few distinct values, otherwise a full scan. Put equality-filtered columns first and range-filtered columns after them.
lessons.example:
WITH txn AS (
  SELECT 'SB1' acct_no, DATE '2026-11-03' txn_date, 5000 amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'SB1', DATE '2026-11-18', 1200 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'SB2', DATE '2026-11-05', 800 FROM dual
)
-- on a real table, an index on (acct_no, txn_date) serves this filter well
SELECT * FROM txn
WHERE acct_no = 'SB1'
  AND txn_date >= DATE '2026-11-01' AND txn_date < DATE '2026-12-01';
lessons.gotcha: An index on (acct_no, txn_date) does not help much a query that filters only on txn_date.
lessons.line: I put equality columns first and the range column last, so one index range scan answers the query.

lessons.why: A number compared with a text column can silently stop Oracle from using an index, a classic interview trap.
lessons.simple: Imagine a library where books are sorted by their written titles. If you ask for a book by a number, the librarian has to read every title and turn it into a number before comparing. That is slow. When a text column is compared with a number, Oracle does the same thing to every row.
lessons.remember: Compare text with text, numbers with numbers.
lessons.explain: When types differ, Oracle converts one side; between VARCHAR2 and NUMBER it converts the character side to NUMBER. So WHERE acct_no = 1001 on a VARCHAR2 column becomes TO_NUMBER(acct_no) = 1001, which is applied to every row and blocks a normal index on acct_no. It can also raise ORA-01722 if any row holds a non-numeric value like 'SB1001'. Writing acct_no = '1001' keeps the index usable, and dates should be compared with DATE or TO_DATE values, not strings.
lessons.example:
WITH acct AS (
  SELECT '1001' acct_no, 25000 bal FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT '1002', 8000 FROM dual
)
-- good: text compared with text, an index on acct_no can be used
SELECT * FROM acct
WHERE acct_no = '1001';
lessons.gotcha: WHERE acct_no = 1001 on a VARCHAR2 column can fail with ORA-01722 once a row like 'SB1001' arrives.
lessons.line: I match literal and bind types to the column type, because implicit TO_NUMBER on the column disables its index.

lessons.why: Interviewers ask why WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= 3 fails and how to fix it.
lessons.simple: Imagine a race where you first decide who is allowed to run, and only after the race do you hand out positions. You cannot use the finishing position to decide who runs. WHERE picks the runners; window functions give positions later. So to keep the top three, you look at the results after the race, in an outer query.
lessons.remember: Filter on a window result from the outside.
lessons.explain: Oracle evaluates FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING before computing analytic functions in the SELECT list. That is why a window function is not allowed in WHERE or HAVING (ORA-30483). To filter on it, compute it in an inline view or CTE and filter in the outer query. Only ORDER BY, which runs last, can reference the window result directly.
lessons.example:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT 'A' AS acct, 500 AS amt FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'B', 900 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'C', 700 FROM dual
)
SELECT acct, amt, rn
FROM  (SELECT acct, amt, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amt DESC) AS rn FROM t)
WHERE  rn <= 2;
lessons.gotcha: Filtering in WHERE before the window changes the window's input, so moving a condition inside or outside the subquery can change the ranks.
lessons.line: Window functions are computed after WHERE, so I rank in a CTE and filter on the rank outside.

lessons.why: Interest, EMI and date cut-offs in banking depend on whether you round or cut off.
lessons.simple: Think of a shopkeeper with ₹99.60. Rounding says "call it ₹100"; cutting off says "just ₹99". ROUND goes to the nearest value, TRUNC simply chops off the extra part. Both also work on dates: TRUNC takes a date-time back to midnight.
lessons.remember: ROUND = nearest; TRUNC = chop, never up.
lessons.explain: ROUND(n, d) rounds to d decimal places, half away from zero, so ROUND(2.5) is 3 and ROUND(-2.5) is -3. TRUNC(n, d) just removes digits after d places, moving toward zero, so TRUNC(-2.7) is -2. A negative d works to the left of the decimal point, such as ROUND(12345, -2) = 12300. On dates, TRUNC(d) gives midnight and TRUNC(d, 'MM') the first of the month, while ROUND(d, 'MM') moves to the nearest month start.
lessons.example:
WITH t AS (SELECT 1234.567 AS amt, -2.5 AS neg,
                  TO_DATE('20-11-2026 18:45','DD-MM-YYYY HH24:MI') AS dt FROM dual)
SELECT ROUND(amt, 2) AS r2,          -- 1234.57
       TRUNC(amt, 2) AS t2,          -- 1234.56
       ROUND(amt, -2) AS r_hundred,  -- 1200
       ROUND(neg) AS r_neg,          -- -3
       TRUNC(dt) AS day_start,       -- 20-11-2026 00:00
       ROUND(dt, 'MM') AS near_month -- 01-12-2026
FROM t;
lessons.gotcha: TRUNC on a negative number moves toward zero, so it is not the same as FLOOR.
lessons.line: I use ROUND for amounts shown to customers and TRUNC where the business rule says to cut off, such as interest paid in whole rupees.

lessons.why: Picking the wrong one silently drops rows or wastes a sort on big reports.
lessons.simple: Imagine two class lists being joined into one. UNION ALL just staples the pages together, even if a child is on both lists. UNION also crosses out repeated names, which takes extra time.
lessons.remember: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps everything, faster.
lessons.explain: UNION ALL appends the result of the second query to the first with no extra work. UNION additionally removes duplicate rows across the whole combined result, which needs a sort or hash step. Duplicates are compared on all selected columns, and NULLs are treated as equal for this purpose. Use UNION ALL when the sets cannot overlap or when duplicates are meaningful, such as summing transactions.
lessons.example:
WITH a AS (SELECT 'Pune' AS city FROM dual UNION ALL SELECT 'Delhi' FROM dual),
     b AS (SELECT 'Pune' AS city FROM dual)
SELECT city FROM a
UNION ALL          -- returns Pune, Delhi, Pune; UNION would return Delhi, Pune
SELECT city FROM b;
lessons.gotcha: UNION also removes duplicates that exist inside a single query, not just across the two.
lessons.line: I default to UNION ALL and use UNION only when I really need distinct rows, because UNION adds a sort.

lessons.why: Interviewers ask this to check that you know when a subquery depends on the outer row.
lessons.simple: A non-correlated subquery is like checking the class average once and comparing everyone to it. A correlated subquery is like checking each child against the average of their own section, so it is re-checked for every child.
lessons.remember: Correlated = the subquery peeks at the outer row.
lessons.explain: A non-correlated subquery does not reference outer columns, so it can be evaluated once and reused. A correlated subquery references a column of the outer query, so logically it runs once per outer row. Oracle often rewrites correlated subqueries into joins (unnesting), so the plan may not be row-by-row. EXISTS and NOT EXISTS are usually written as correlated subqueries.
lessons.example:
WITH emp AS (
  SELECT 'Asha' name, 'IT' dept, 90 sal FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Ravi', 'IT', 60 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Neha', 'HR', 50 FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Kiran', 'HR', 40 FROM dual)
SELECT name, dept, sal
FROM   emp e
WHERE  sal > (SELECT AVG(sal) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept);
lessons.gotcha: A correlated subquery in SELECT that returns more than one row raises ORA-01427 at run time.
lessons.line: A correlated subquery depends on the outer row, but the optimizer can unnest it into a join, so I always check the plan.

lessons.why: After any INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or SELECT INTO, PL/SQL tells you what happened through SQL% attributes.
lessons.simple: After you post letters, the post office gives you a receipt saying how many went out. SQL%ROWCOUNT is that receipt for the last SQL statement. SQL%FOUND says 'yes, at least one', and SQL%NOTFOUND says 'none at all'.
lessons.remember: SQL%ROWCOUNT = receipt for the last DML.
lessons.explain: Every DML statement and SELECT INTO in PL/SQL runs through an implicit cursor named SQL. SQL%ROWCOUNT returns the number of rows affected, SQL%FOUND is TRUE if at least one row was affected, and SQL%NOTFOUND is the opposite. An UPDATE or DELETE that matches no rows does not raise an error; it simply sets SQL%ROWCOUNT to 0. The attributes always describe the most recent statement, so read them immediately after the DML you care about.
lessons.example:
WITH stock AS (
  SELECT 'S1' store_id, 'RICE5KG' sku, 30 qty FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT 'S1', 'OIL1L', 12 FROM dual
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_an_update_would_touch
FROM   stock
WHERE  store_id = 'S1' AND sku = 'ATTA10KG';
-- 0 rows: in PL/SQL, UPDATE with this WHERE sets SQL%ROWCOUNT = 0
lessons.gotcha: A call to a procedure, a COMMIT or another DML between your statement and the check overwrites SQL%ROWCOUNT, so capture it into a variable right away.
lessons.line: I check SQL%ROWCOUNT right after an UPDATE to detect a missing row, since zero rows updated is not an exception in Oracle.

lessons.why: Interviewers love asking which one to use and how each treats NULL.
lessons.simple: DECODE and CASE are both like a choose-your-answer card: if this, say that. DECODE is the old short version that only checks 'is it equal'. CASE is the newer, more flexible one that can also check bigger-than, smaller-than and more. One surprise: DECODE thinks two empty boxes are equal, but a simple CASE does not.
lessons.remember: DECODE treats NULL = NULL; simple CASE does not.
lessons.explain: DECODE(expr, s1, r1, s2, r2, default) is Oracle-only and works only in SQL, comparing with equality. CASE is ANSI standard, works in SQL and PL/SQL, and its searched form (CASE WHEN cond THEN ...) supports ranges, LIKE and multiple columns. DECODE considers two NULLs equal, while CASE expr WHEN NULL never matches because NULL = NULL is unknown; use CASE WHEN expr IS NULL instead. Both stop at the first match and return NULL when nothing matches and no default or ELSE is given.
lessons.example:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT 'Pune' AS city FROM dual UNION ALL
  SELECT NULL         FROM dual
)
SELECT city,
       DECODE(city, NULL, 'missing', 'ok')          AS via_decode,
       CASE city WHEN NULL THEN 'missing' ELSE 'ok' END AS via_simple_case,
       CASE WHEN city IS NULL THEN 'missing' ELSE 'ok' END AS via_searched_case
FROM   t;
lessons.gotcha: CASE city WHEN NULL THEN ... never fires; the NULL row returns 'ok' in the simple CASE column.
lessons.line: I use searched CASE for readability and portability, and I remember that DECODE matches NULL to NULL while CASE needs IS NULL.
